title: Seeds that wait: how a dry seed stays alive for years

summary.text: Put dry moong seeds in the freezer for a night, and nearly all of them still sprout. Soak the same seeds first, and one night in the freezer kills them. A dry seed holds so little water that no ice forms inside. This is how a lotus seed stayed alive for about 1,300 years. It is also how seed banks keep seeds alive for a hundred years or more. Your child runs the Freezer Test. Then they test whether a seed that has started to wake can be dried again. They also learn how a seed bank dries, freezes, tests and regrows seeds.
summary.art: Two steel plates side by side on wet cloths: one with green moong seeds that all have white roots, one with dark, soft moong seeds and no roots, and a freezer door open behind them.

intro.hook: A scientist in the United States was given a lotus seed from a dry lake bed in China. The seed was about 1,300 years old. She filed a small cut in the hard coat and put the seed in water. Within a few days the seed had a green shoot. How can a seed stay alive for 1,300 years?
intro.text: The scientist was Jane Shen-Miller, and she reported the lotus seed in 1995. The seed had done almost nothing for all those years. They had not grown, and they had hardly used any food. Then water reached the young plant inside, and the seed germinated like a seed from last year. In this unit you find out what keeps a dry seed alive. You put dry seeds and soaked seeds in the freezer. You dry seeds again after they have started to wake. Then you see how seed banks use the same science to keep seeds safe.
intro.art: A dark brown, oval lotus seed with a small filed cut in the coat, lying in a shallow dish of water with a short green shoot coming out.

outcomes: I can name the parts of a seed and say, in order, what happens when a seed germinates.
I can plan a fair germination test: what to change, what to measure and what to keep the same.
I can turn a count into a germination percentage, and explain why a test needs many seeds and many days.
I can explain why a dry seed lives through freezing and a soaked seed does not.
I can explain why a seed can be dried again before the root comes out, but not after.
I can explain what dormancy is, and give examples of seeds that waited for many years.
I can describe how a seed bank keeps seeds alive, and why the bank must test and regrow them.
I can give reasons for keeping seeds in frozen banks and reasons for keeping them growing in farmers' fields.

terms.meaning: The start of growth in a seed. The seed takes in water and swells, the seed coat splits, and the first root comes out.
terms.example: A moong seed on a wet cloth germinates in about a day. You can see a small white root.
terms.art: A green moong seed with a split coat and a short white root pointing down.

terms.meaning: The young plant inside a seed. The embryo has a tiny root, a tiny shoot and one or two seed leaves.
terms.example: Open a soaked chana. The small pointed bump at one end is the embryo's root.
terms.art: A chana opened in two halves, with an arrow pointing at the tiny plant at one end.

terms.meaning: The skin around a seed. The seed coat protects the embryo and controls how fast water gets in.
terms.example: The green skin of a moong seed and the red skin of a rajma are seed coats.
terms.art: A soaked rajma with the red skin half peeled away from the pale inside.

terms.meaning: The food that the parent plant packed into the seed. In beans and dals, the food is in two thick seed leaves called cotyledons.
terms.example: The two halves of a chana are cotyledons. The embryo lives on this food until the first green leaves work.
terms.art: The two fat halves of a bean, shaded to show they are full of food, joined to a tiny shoot and root.

terms.meaning: The radicle is the embryo's first root. The plumule is the embryo's first shoot. The radicle always comes out first.
terms.example: The white tail on a moong sprout is the radicle. The plumule comes up a day or two later.
terms.art: A sprouting bean with the root labelled radicle and the small folded shoot labelled plumule.

terms.meaning: Alive and able to germinate. A viable seed may be dry and still for years.
terms.example: Dry moong in a jar are viable. Boiled moong look the same, but they are no longer viable.
terms.art: Two heaps of moong that look the same, one with a tick and one with a cross.

terms.meaning: Alive, but not germinating. Some seeds stay dormant even when they have water, warmth and air.
terms.example: A lotus seed can lie dormant in wet mud for hundreds of years, because water cannot pass the hard coat.
terms.art: A hard brown lotus seed lying in wet mud with no shoot.

terms.meaning: Anything in a test that can change. In a fair test you change one variable, measure one variable, and keep all the others the same.
terms.example: In the Freezer Test, one variable you change is whether the seeds go into the freezer.
terms.art: Three small labels on a notebook page: change, measure, keep the same.

terms.meaning: The group in a test that gets the ordinary treatment. You compare every other group with the control.
terms.example: In the Freezer Test, the dry seeds kept on the shelf are the control group.
terms.art: Four plates of seeds with one plate marked with a star as the control.

terms.meaning: How many seeds out of every 100 germinate in a test.
terms.example: If 18 of 20 seeds germinate, that is 90 out of 100, or 90 percent.
terms.art: A plate of 20 seeds, 18 with roots and 2 without, and the label 90%.

terms.meaning: A small number of seeds taken from a big batch and tested, to find out about the whole batch.
terms.example: A seed bank tests a sample of 50 or 100 seeds. The rest of the seeds stay in the freezer.
terms.art: A big sack of seeds with a small spoonful taken out and laid in rows.

terms.meaning: How much of a seed's weight is water.
terms.example: A dry moong seed is about one tenth water. A moong sprout is more than three quarters water.
terms.art: A seed drawn as a bar with a small blue part for water, beside a sprout whose bar is mostly blue.

terms.meaning: A small, sharp-edged piece of ice that forms when water freezes.
terms.example: When a soaked seed freezes, ice crystals form inside the cells and tear them.
terms.art: A zoom-in on a plant cell with sharp ice crystals poking through the cell's thin skin.

terms.meaning: A place that keeps seeds of many kinds of plants alive for a long time. The seeds are dried, sealed and frozen.
terms.example: India's National Genebank in New Delhi keeps more than 4 lakh seed samples in cold rooms.
terms.art: Shelves of sealed silver packets in a cold room, with a worker in a thick jacket.

terms.meaning: All the living seeds lying in the soil of a place, waiting to germinate.
terms.example: Weeds that come up in a pot where you sowed nothing grew from the soil seed bank.
terms.art: A cut-away view of soil with many tiny seeds scattered at different depths.

terms.meaning: To sow some stored seeds, grow the plants, and collect fresh seeds to put back in the bank.
terms.example: When fewer than 85 in 100 stored seeds germinate, a seed bank regrows the sample.
terms.art: A sealed seed packet with an arrow to a row of plants, and an arrow from the plants to a new packet.

explanations.concept: Inside a seed, and the steps of germination
explanations.definition: A seed has three parts: a seed coat, an embryo and a food store. Germination is the start of growth, and its steps always come in the same order.
explanations.description: The seed coat is the skin. The embryo is the young plant, with a first root called the radicle and a first shoot called the plumule. The food store feeds the embryo. In beans and dals the food is in two thick seed leaves called cotyledons. Germination has five steps. First, the seed takes in water and swells. Second, the seed coat splits. Third, the radicle grows out and turns downwards. Fourth, the plumule grows upwards. Fifth, the first green leaves open and start to make food. Until then the seedling lives only on the food store, so the cotyledons shrink as the seedling grows. This is why a seed can germinate in the dark.
examples: Soak a chana overnight and open the two halves. The tiny pointed embryo sits at one end.
A moong seed on a wet cloth shows a split coat and a white radicle in about one day.
The two thick halves of a moong sprout shrivel after a week, because the food has been used.
explanations.art: Five small drawings in a row: a dry bean, a swollen bean, a bean with a split coat and a root, a bean with a root and a shoot, and a seedling with two green leaves.

explanations.concept: What a seed needs to germinate, and how a fair test shows it
explanations.definition: Most seeds need three things to germinate: water, oxygen from the air, and enough warmth. Most seeds do not need light or soil.
explanations.description: Water softens the coat and starts the chemistry inside the embryo. Oxygen lets the embryo release energy from the food store. This is called respiration, and it is why seeds under deep water often fail. Warmth sets the speed. Moong germinate fastest at about 25 to 35 degrees Celsius, and hardly at all in a fridge. A fair test finds these needs one at a time. A variable is anything that can change in a test. You change one variable, such as water or no water. You measure one variable, such as how many seeds have a root. You keep every other variable the same: the kind of seed, the number, the cloth and the place. The group with the ordinary treatment is the control group. A few kinds of seed also need light. Lettuce seeds and many tiny weed seeds germinate only after light has reached them.
examples: Dry moong on a dry cloth: none germinate. The same moong on a wet cloth: nearly all germinate.
Moong on a wet cloth in the fridge: very few germinate until the cup is moved to a shelf.
Moong in a dark cupboard germinate as well as moong by a window.
explanations.art: Five labelled jars of seeds: dry, wet, wet in a fridge, wet in a dark box, and under water with a layer of oil.

explanations.concept: Why a test needs many seeds, many days and a percentage
explanations.definition: A germination test uses a sample of many seeds and runs for several days. The result is given as a percentage, which is the number that germinate out of every 100.
explanations.description: In any batch, a few seeds are dead or damaged before the test begins. With 2 seeds in a group, one dead seed changes the result from 100 percent to 50 percent. With 20 seeds, one dead seed changes the result by only 5 percent. So a bigger sample gives a steadier answer. Seeds also wake at different times, so a count on day 1 can miss seeds that wake on day 3. A test must run until no more seeds are waking. A percentage lets you compare groups of different sizes. For 18 of 20 seeds, each seed is worth 5 percent, so 18 seeds make 90 percent. A result that does not fit the pattern is called an odd result, or an anomalous result. Scientists write odd results down and repeat the test. They never rub them out.
examples: 18 of 20 seeds is 90 percent. 41 of 50 seeds is 82 percent.
Seed labs test 100 seeds at a time, often four lots of 100.
Seed packets in India print the germination percentage and the date of the test.
explanations.art: A cloth with 20 seeds in four neat rows of 5, most with roots, and a notebook showing 18 out of 20 equals 90 percent.

explanations.concept: A dry seed: alive, with almost no water
explanations.definition: A dry seed is alive, but nearly all activity inside has stopped. This is possible because the seed holds very little water.
explanations.description: While a seed ripens on the parent plant, the seed dries out on purpose. A stored moong seed is only about one tenth water. Your body is more than half water, and a moong sprout is more than three quarters water. Before drying, the embryo fills their cells with sugars and protective proteins. As the last water leaves, this mixture sets hard, a little like hard-boiled sugar candy. Scientists call this the glassy state. In a glass, molecules can hardly move, so the chemical reactions of life almost stop. The embryo uses almost no food and wears out very slowly. When water comes back, the glass softens within hours, and the reactions start again. Tardigrades, which are tiny water animals, and some mosses and ferns can dry out and wait in the same way.
examples: Dry moong, rajma and wheat in kitchen jars are alive and waiting.
Sanjeevani, a small fern relative sold dry in Indian markets, turns green again in a bowl of water.
A dried tardigrade can start moving again after years, once water returns.
explanations.art: A zoom-in on a dry seed cell drawn as a solid, clear block with parts held still inside, beside a wet cell with parts moving about.

explanations.concept: Why freezing kills a soaked seed and spares a dry seed
explanations.definition: Freezing harms living cells when the water inside them turns to ice. A dry seed has too little free water to make ice, so cold does not harm them.
explanations.description: Water grows bigger when it freezes, and it forms sharp crystals. A soaked seed is full of water. In a freezer, ice crystals form inside the cells. The crystals tear the thin skins, called membranes, around each cell and inside it. When the seed thaws, the cells leak and die. A dry seed holds only a little water, and that water is held tightly inside the glassy mixture. No ice crystals form, so nothing is torn. Cold then helps the seed, because cold slows the slow wearing out even more. So the result depends on two variables together. Cold alone does not kill the seed. Water alone does not kill the seed. Cold and water together do.
examples: Dry wheat seeds in a seed bank stay alive at minus 18 degrees Celsius for many decades.
Frozen green peas from a shop do not grow, because they were wet when they were frozen.
A wet leaf of palak left in the freezer turns limp and dark when it thaws.
explanations.art: Two zoom-in circles: a wet cell pierced by sharp ice crystals, and a dry cell with no crystals, both under a snowflake sign.

explanations.concept: The point of no return: when a waking seed can no longer be dried
explanations.definition: A seed can be soaked and dried again safely for the first few hours. Once the radicle has come out, drying kills the seedling.
explanations.description: The embryo keeps their protection for the first hours of soaking. If the seed dries again in that time, the glassy state forms again and the seed waits. Farmers use this. Many soak seeds overnight, dry the surface and then sow, so the seeds come up faster. This is called seed priming. Once the radicle grows out, the embryo has changed. The new cells are large and full of water. The protective sugars and proteins have been used or taken apart. If these cells dry, they collapse and die. So germination has a point of no return, at about the time the root appears. A seed that wakes just before a long dry spell cannot go back to waiting. This is why the timing of waking matters so much to a plant.
examples: Moong soaked for 6 hours and dried for 2 days usually germinate well when wetted again.
Moong with roots 1 centimetre long, dried for 2 days, usually do not grow again.
Seedlings that come up after one light shower often die if no more rain follows.
explanations.art: A timeline arrow: a dry seed, a swollen seed marked 'can still be dried', then a seed with a root and a red line marked 'no way back'.

explanations.concept: Dormancy: seeds that wait even when they have water
explanations.definition: A dormant seed is alive but does not germinate, even with water, warmth and air. Dormancy keeps a seed from waking at a bad time.
explanations.description: A dry seed in a jar waits because there is no water. Scientists call that resting. Dormancy is different, because a dormant seed waits even on wet soil. Some dormant seeds have a coat that water cannot pass, such as lotus and tamarind. Others hold chemical signals that stop the embryo until a sign arrives. The sign may be a cold season, light, or a heavy rain. Because germination cannot be undone, waiting for the right sign protects the seedling. Dormant seeds collect in the ground. All the living seeds in the soil of a place are called the soil seed bank. Some of them wait for one season, and some wait for many years.
examples: A lotus seed's coat is so hard that the seed can lie in wet mud for centuries.
Apple seeds germinate only after some weeks of cold, which tells them winter has passed.
Dig up a patch of bare soil, and weeds soon appear from seeds that were buried there.
explanations.art: A cut-away of pond mud with a hard lotus seed lying still, and a second lotus seed with a cracked coat sending up a shoot.

explanations.concept: How long can a seed wait?
explanations.description: Nobody knows the longest time a seed can stay alive. The answer is different for every kind of seed, and for every place the seed is kept. In ordinary kitchen storage, onion seeds last a year or two, and moong lasts several years. The oldest seeds known to have germinated were kept dry or sealed by nature. A date palm seed about 2,000 years old, from the desert fortress of Masada, germinated in 2005. A lotus seed about 1,300 years old, from a dry lake bed in China, germinated in the 1990s. Seeds die in the end because damage slowly builds up, even in the glassy state. The instructions in their DNA break in places, and the cell membranes become leaky. A waking seed repairs this damage in the first hours. When there is too much damage to repair, the seed can no longer germinate.
examples: Moth mullein seeds buried in a bottle in 1879 still germinated in 2021, after 142 years.
Lotus seedlings grown from very old seeds sometimes had odd leaves, a sign of old damage.
Mango and jackfruit seeds die within weeks, because they cannot survive drying at all.
explanations.art: A long timeline with three seeds on it: a small mullein seed at 142 years, a lotus seed at 1,300 years and a date seed at 2,000 years.

explanations.concept: How a seed bank keeps seeds alive
explanations.definition: A seed bank keeps seeds viable for a long time by keeping them very dry and very cold. Then it tests them and regrows them before they die.
explanations.description: A seed bank follows six steps. First, the seeds are collected, with a note of the place and the date. Second, they are cleaned and a sample is tested for germination. Third, they are dried slowly in a cool, dry room for some weeks. By the end they are only about one twentieth water. Fourth, they are sealed in packets that no air or damp can enter. Fifth, they are stored at about minus 18 degrees Celsius, which is the cold of a home freezer. Sixth, a sample is taken out every five or ten years and tested. Before a packet is opened, it is left closed until it reaches room temperature. Otherwise damp from the air would settle on the cold seeds. If fewer than about 85 in 100 germinate, the bank sows the seeds. The plants are grown, and the fresh seeds are stored. A seed bank also sends copies to other banks. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway opened in 2008. More than 13 lakh copies from banks around the world are kept there.
examples: India's National Genebank in New Delhi stores more than 4 lakh seed samples.
The Millennium Seed Bank in England stores seeds of more than 40,000 kinds of wild plants.
In 2015, scientists who had to leave Aleppo in Syria took back their copies from Svalbard and regrew them.
explanations.art: Six small pictures in a row: collecting seed heads, cleaning, a drying room, sealing a silver packet, a freezer room, and a germination test on paper.

explanations.concept: Frozen banks or living fields: two ways to save seeds
explanations.definition: People agree that old crop varieties must be saved. They disagree about which matters more: frozen seed banks, or farmers who keep sowing the seeds.
explanations.description: A frozen seed is safe from floods, pests and war, but the seed does not change. The world outside keeps changing: new pests arrive, and the weather shifts. A crop that farmers sow every year keeps adapting. Each year, the plants that do well leave the most seed. But a field can be lost in one bad season. Some seeds cannot be frozen at all, because they die when they are dried. Mango, jackfruit and cocoa are like this, and they are kept as living trees.
examples: Rahibai Popere, a farmer in Maharashtra, has saved many old crop varieties by growing and sharing them.
Women farmers of the Deccan Development Society in Telangana run village seed banks of millets. Seed is lent, and paid back after harvest.
After the tsunami of 2004, farmers in Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu went back to old paddy that stands salty soil.

perspectives.who: Scientists who run frozen seed banks
perspectives.explanation: A freezer keeps thousands of varieties in one small room for a hundred years, at low cost. When a variety is lost from the fields, the bank can give it back. No village could keep growing so many varieties every year.

perspectives.who: Farmers and scientists who keep seeds growing, such as the ecologist Debal Deb in Odisha
perspectives.explanation: A seed in a freezer stops adapting to new weather and new pests. A variety also needs farmers who know how to grow, cook and choose that crop. So the seeds should be sown every year, in many fields.

perspectives.who: Many people who work with both
perspectives.explanation: The two ways cover each other's risks. Fields keep seeds adapting, and frozen banks are the back-up when a field is lost.

explanations.art: A split picture: a cold room with sealed packets on one side, and women farmers sorting seeds on a mat beside a millet field on the other.

explanations.concept: Is a dry seed alive while nothing is happening inside?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that a dry seed can live again. They disagree about what to call the seed while almost nothing is happening inside.
explanations.description: In the driest, coldest seeds, scientists can find almost no activity at all. No growth, no feeding, and almost no respiration can be measured. Yet the seed germinates when water returns. The biologist David Keilin gave this state a name in 1959. He called it cryptobiosis, which means hidden life.
examples: A dry tardigrade and a dry seed both show almost no activity, and both can become active again.
A boiled seed shows no activity either, but can never become active again.

perspectives.who: Biologists who say life is something a body does
perspectives.explanation: Living means taking in food, respiring and repairing. A seed that does none of these is not living at that time. The seed keeps the ability to live, and that ability is what a boiled seed has lost.

perspectives.who: Biologists who say life is something a body keeps
perspectives.explanation: The seed keeps all the parts and all the order needed for life, and guards them. Keeping that order through 1,000 years is itself what the living seed is doing. So the seed is alive all the time.

explanations.art: A dry seed in the centre of a page with a question mark above, and a faint outline of a full-grown plant drawn around the seed.

explanations.description: A dry seed can live through more than a freezer. From 2008 to 2009, scientists kept seeds of two small plants outside the International Space Station. The seeds stayed there for 18 months. The seeds had no air. They met strong ultraviolet light from the Sun, and they went from very hot to very cold on every orbit. Back on Earth, some of the seeds still germinated. The dark colours in the seed coat had shielded the embryo from the ultraviolet light. Some scientists ask whether dry seeds or spores could carry life from one planet to another. This is only an idea. Nobody has found any sign that it has happened.
examples: Tobacco and thale cress seeds germinated after 18 months outside the space station.
Dry seeds have been flown to the Moon's orbit and grown afterwards on Earth.
explanations.art: A small tray of seeds fixed to the outside of a space station, with the Earth far below.

agreed.text: A seed germinates in a fixed order: water goes in, the seed swells, the coat splits, the root comes out, and then the shoot.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch this on a wet cloth or through the side of a glass jar. Time-lapse films of many kinds of seed show the same order.

agreed.text: Most seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate. Most seeds do not need light.
agreed.evidence: Fair tests that change one variable at a time give the same result all over the world. Seeds in the dark germinate. Seeds without water, without air or in the cold do not.

agreed.text: A dry seed lives through freezing, and a soaked seed does not.
agreed.evidence: Seed banks freeze dry seeds at minus 18 degrees Celsius and germinate them decades later. The Freezer Test shows the same thing at home in five days.

agreed.text: Drier and colder seeds live longer.
agreed.evidence: Seed scientists have stored batches of seeds at many levels of dryness and cold, and tested samples for years. The drier, colder batches kept their germination longest.

agreed.text: Some seeds can stay alive for more than a thousand years.
agreed.evidence: A lotus seed and a date palm seed were dated by a test called carbon dating, which measures age. Both seeds were then germinated.

agreed.text: Stored seeds slowly die, even when frozen, so seed banks must test them and regrow them.
agreed.evidence: Seed banks that have tested the same samples for decades see the germination percentage fall. Some kinds fall within a few decades, and others take far longer.

challenging.for: Frost kills seedlings and young plants. Wet seeds left out on a freezing night do die.
challenging.against: Cold kills only when there is water inside to turn into ice. Dry seeds live through a freezer, and seed banks depend on this.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that cold always harms seeds.

challenging.claim: Wheat found in the tombs of ancient Egypt can still grow.
challenging.who: Many people in Europe in the 1800s, and some sellers of 'mummy wheat' since then.
challenging.for: Travellers said they had sown grain from tombs and seen it grow. Seeds do live for a long time when they are dry.
challenging.against: Botanists who tested grain that truly came from tombs never saw one grain germinate. The grain was brown and brittle. The wheat that grew had been mixed in later.
challenging.context: This card is about an old claim that wheat grains about 3,000 years old had germinated.

challenging.claim: Once seeds are in a frozen vault, that crop is safe for ever.
challenging.who: A common belief about seed banks.
challenging.for: Dry, frozen seeds can live for a hundred years or more, and a vault is safe from floods and pests.
challenging.against: Frozen seeds still age slowly, and some kinds die within decades. A bank must keep testing and regrowing its seeds. That needs fields, money and skilled people.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that a frozen seed vault needs no further work.

challenging.claim: The best seed bank is a farmer's field, not a freezer.
challenging.who: Many farmers' groups and some ecologists.
challenging.for: Seeds sown every year keep adapting to new weather and pests. The knowledge of how to grow them stays alive too.
challenging.against: A flood, a drought or a war can wipe out a field in one season. Without a frozen copy, the variety is lost.
challenging.context: This card is about a real disagreement over where seeds are safest.

challenging.claim: A fully dry seed is not alive. It is only able to become alive.
challenging.who: Some biologists who study dried and frozen life.
challenging.for: In the driest seeds, no feeding, growth or respiration can be measured.
challenging.against: The seed keeps and protects every part needed for life, and a dead seed does not. Many biologists call that being alive.
challenging.context: This card is about what to call a seed while almost nothing is happening inside.

big_questions.q: A dry seed and a boiled seed both do nothing in a jar. One is alive and one is dead. What is the difference between them?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each seed still has inside, and what happens to each when water arrives.

big_questions.q: A seedling cannot go back to being a seed. What other changes in living things cannot be undone?
big_questions.hint: Think about an egg that has hatched, a flower that has opened, or a tooth that has fallen out.

big_questions.q: In the Freezer Test, neither cold alone nor water alone killed the seeds. Can a cause be two things together?
big_questions.hint: Think about a wet floor and running. Which one makes you slip?

big_questions.q: During a war in the 1940s, hungry scientists in Leningrad guarded sacks of seed and did not eat them. Why would seeds matter that much?
big_questions.hint: The seeds were thousands of crop varieties collected by Nikolai Vavilov. Think about who would need them after the war.

big_questions.q: A seed bank stops seeds from germinating for a hundred years. Is that done for the seeds, or for us?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a seed would do without us. Then think about what the plants gain when a lost variety is sown again.

big_questions.q: Farmers bred every crop over thousands of years, and nobody knows their names. Who should own the seeds in a seed bank?
big_questions.hint: In the Svalbard vault, each box still belongs to the bank that sent it. Is that fair to the farmers?

story.title: The Pot Under the Roof
story.note: Thenmozhi, Paatti, Selvam Maama and their village are made up. These things are real. On 26 December 2004 a tsunami sent sea water over the fields of Nagapattinam district in Tamil Nadu. The salt stayed in the soil. Afterwards, farmers there went back to old paddy varieties that can grow in salty soil. Many families kept seed paddy in sealed mud pots with dried neem leaves. Counting 100 seeds onto a wet cloth is the test that farmers and seed labs really use. The numbers in Thenmozhi's count are made up.
text: The sea came into Thenmozhi's village on a Sunday morning in December. By evening the water had gone back. The salt had not.

Nine months later, the family's paddy field still showed it. In the nursery bed, the seedlings from the shop seed had come up green. Then they had turned yellow from the tips, and then brown. Selvam Maama pulled up a seedling and held the little plant out. The roots were short and dark.
"Salt," he said. "The rain has not washed enough of it out. And I have no money for a second sack."
Paatti said nothing. She fetched the ladder, and she pointed at the roof.

Under the palm-leaf roof, tied to a rafter, hung a mud pot. The sea had filled the house to the height of Thenmozhi's chest that Sunday. The pot had hung above the water. The mouth was closed with a clay lid, and the lid was sealed with mud.
Maama brought the pot down. Paatti broke the seal with her thumbnail. Inside lay dry neem leaves, and under them paddy. The grains were darker than shop paddy, with long, stiff hairs at the tips.
"My mother grew this in the low field by the backwater," said Paatti. "The backwater is half sea. This paddy never minded."
"When did you fill this pot?" asked Maama.
"Two harvests ago."

Maama let the grains run through his fingers. "Twenty months, Amma. Through two monsoons, in this wet air. This is not seed any more. This is bird feed." He looked at the sky. "And if I sow the nursery from this pot and nothing comes up, the season is gone. There is no time to sow twice."
Thenmozhi picked up one grain and bit down. The grain was hard, and cracked between her teeth like a tiny stick.
"They are very dry," she said.
"Dry is not the same as alive," said Maama.
He was right about that, and Thenmozhi knew it. A dead grain and a living grain look the same. She turned the grain over. There was no way to see inside.
"Soak them," said Maama. "Soak the whole pot tonight. If they swell and sprout, we sow. If they rot, we know."
"And if they sprout, and then no rain comes for the field?" said Paatti. "A sprouted grain cannot go back into the pot, Selvam. Once the root is out, you sow that day or you lose them."
Maama had no answer. They stood around the pot. Thousands of grains lay in it, and nobody could ask them.

Thenmozhi looked at the grain in her hand. One grain could not speak for the pot. One grain might be the only dead one, or the only living one. But the pot was all the same harvest, dried on the same mat, sealed on the same day.
"We do not have to wake them all," she said slowly. "We can wake some. A hundred."
"And waste a hundred grains?"
"A hundred is half a handful, Maama. The pot holds thousands. The hundred will tell us about the rest."
Paatti was already tearing a square from an old gunny sack.

Thenmozhi wet the sack cloth and wrung it out. She stirred the pot with her arm, right to the bottom, and took grains from the top, the middle and the deep part. She counted them onto the cloth in rows of ten. Ten rows. She rolled the cloth up like a mat, tied it with a strip of banana fibre, and stood it in a tumbler in the corner where the cooking fire kept the wall warm.
On the second day she unrolled it. Nothing. The grains looked exactly as before, only darker with the wet.
"Bird feed," said Maama, and went out to the field.
On the third day, twelve grains had a white point at one end, no longer than an ant.
On the fifth day she counted fifty-eight.

On the seventh day she counted three times, moving each sprouted grain to one side of the cloth so that none was counted twice. Seventy-one grains had a root and a pale green spike. Twenty-nine lay as they had lain on the first day.
Maama squatted beside the cloth. "Twenty-nine dead," he said.
"Seventy-one alive," said Thenmozhi. "After twenty months. Out of every ten grains, seven will grow. So where you would sow seven, sow ten."
Maama looked at the cloth for a long time. Then he laughed. "So now the pot has spoken," he said. "Through half a handful."
They sowed the nursery bed the next morning, thicker than Maama had ever sown it. The seedlings came up dark green. Thenmozhi went to look at the tips every day. They stayed green.

In January the paddy stood chest high in the field where the shop seedlings had died, and the long hairs on the grains shone in the sun. Paatti filled three pots from the first threshing, before a single grain was sold. One went back under the roof. Two went to the neighbours on either side.
Thenmozhi sealed the lid of their pot with mud. Then she took a piece of charcoal from the hearth. On the side of the pot she wrote the month and the year. Under that she wrote: 71 of 100.
"Next year," she told the pot, "I will ask you again."
story.epiphany: For the parent: nobody can tell a living seed from a dead one by looking. The only way to know is to wake the seed with water, and waking cannot be undone. So Thenmozhi wakes a sample of 100 grains and lets them speak for the whole pot. Her count, 71 of 100, also tells the family how thickly to sow. The paddy was alive after 20 months because the grains were kept dry in a sealed pot.
ask: Maama wanted to soak the whole pot to find out whether the paddy was alive. What was wrong with that plan?
Why did Thenmozhi take grains from the top, the middle and the bottom of the pot?
Would 10 grains have told the family as much as 100? Why or why not?
The paddy in the pot stayed alive for 20 months in damp sea air. What kept the grains alive?
Why did Paatti fill three pots before selling any grain, and give two away?
