games.title: Scoop and Guess: how many seeds must you test?
games.context: In this game a dabba holds 50 seeds. Rajma stand for living seeds and chana stand for dead seeds. You take out a few seeds without looking and guess what percent of the whole dabba is alive.

printables.title: 5 mix cards for the setter: cut them out and keep them face down
Score sheet: one row for each round
items: True percent alive on the mix card
Points: 1 for each guess within 10 of the true percent

rules: You need 45 rajma, 25 kabuli chana, a steel dabba with a lid, a spoon, and the mix cards. A rajma is a living seed. A chana is a dead seed.
One player is the setter. The setter picks a mix card in secret, puts those seeds in the dabba, closes the lid and shakes.
The other player is the guesser. The guesser shuts their eyes, stirs with the spoon and lifts out 5 seeds, one at a time.
The guesser looks at the 5 seeds and says what percent of the whole dabba is alive. The setter writes the guess.
The guesser lifts out 5 more seeds, to make 10, and guesses again. Then 15 more, to make 25, and guesses a third time.
The setter shows the mix card. Each guess within 10 of the true percent scores 1 point. A round can score 3 points.
Put all the seeds back, swap jobs and play again. After 3 rounds each, the player with more points wins.

Playing alone? Use the 80 percent mix. Take 5 seeds and write the percent alive. Put them back and shake. Do this 10 times. Then do 10 scoops of 25 seeds. Count how many scoops of each size came within 10 of 80.

setup.art: A steel dabba with rajma and pale chana mixed inside, a spoon, five small cards face down and a score sheet.
setup.caption: 1. The setter fills the dabba with the mix on a secret card and shakes.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut lifting one seed out of a dabba with a spoon, and four seeds already on a plate.
setup.caption: 2. The guesser lifts out 5 seeds without looking and guesses the percent alive.

setup.art: A plate with 25 seeds sorted into a big heap of rajma and a small heap of chana, beside a card being turned over.
setup.caption: 3. Guess again after 10 seeds and after 25. Then turn over the card.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the mix cards. 2. Count 45 rajma and 25 chana into two bowls. 3. Explain that rajma are living seeds and chana are dead seeds. 4. Practise turning a small count into a percentage.
flow.say: Out of 5 seeds, each seed is worth 20 percent. Out of 10, each is worth 10 percent. Out of 25, each is worth 4 percent. So 4 rajma out of 5 means 80 percent alive.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Count the rajma and chana. Rajma are alive. Chana are dead.
flow.parent: A seed bank has the same problem. It cannot germinate every seed to find out how many are alive. Then no seeds would be left to store.
flow.context: This is the first step of Scoop and Guess. You set up a dabba of rajma and chana that stands for a batch of living and dead seeds.

flow.do: Play two rounds each. After each round, ask the question below.
flow.say: Shut your eyes, stir, and lift out 5 seeds. What percent of the dabba is alive? Now take 5 more. Do you want to change your guess? Now 15 more.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Lift out 5 seeds. Guess the percent alive. Take more seeds. Guess again.

ask.q: Which of your three guesses did you trust most? Why?
good: The guess after 25 seeds, because I had seen half the dabba.
With 5 seeds, one chana changes the answer by 20 percent.

flow.parent: A player who gets 5 rajma out of 5 will often guess 100 percent. Let the game correct that.
flow.context: In this step of Scoop and Guess you take samples of 5, 10 and 25 seeds. Each time you guess how many seeds in the dabba are alive.

flow.do: Finish the rounds. Then count, over all rounds, how many guesses were within 10 after 5 seeds, after 10 and after 25. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Let's count how often each size of sample was close. Which size was right most often? What does that tell a seed lab?
flow.kid: Finish the game. Count which guess was close most often: 5, 10 or 25 seeds.

check.q: A lab tests 100 seeds, not 5, from a big sack. What is the main reason?
options: A bigger sample gives a steadier answer
Small samples take longer to count
check.why: With 5 seeds, one dead seed changes the answer by 20 percent, so luck decides the result. With 100 seeds, one dead seed changes the answer by 1 percent. This is a game moment, so talk about it and play on.

flow.context: This is the last step of Scoop and Guess. You find out which sample size gave the closest guesses about the seeds in the dabba.

games.title: Wake, Wait or Gone? The seed fate cards
games.context: This is a card game about what happens to seeds. Each card describes a seed and what was done to them. You say whether the seed will wake, wait, or is gone.

printables.title: 24 seed fate cards: the seed on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: Dry moong seeds spend one night in a freezer. Then they are put on a wet cloth.
items.b: WAKE. A dry seed holds too little water to make ice, so the cold does no harm.

items.f: Soaked moong seeds spend one night in a freezer. Then they are put on a wet cloth.
items.b: GONE. Ice crystals formed inside the wet cells and tore them.

items.f: Dry moong seeds sit in a closed jar on a kitchen shelf for six months.
items.b: WAIT. With no water the seeds rest, and they stay viable.

items.f: Moong seeds with roots 1 centimetre long are dried for two days. Then they get water.
items.b: GONE. Once the root is out, the seedling cannot survive drying.

items.f: Moong seeds are soaked for 6 hours and dried for two days. Then they get water.
items.b: WAKE. Before the root comes out, a seed can be dried again safely.

items.f: Moong seeds are boiled for ten minutes, cooled and put on a wet cloth.
items.b: GONE. Boiling destroyed the embryo.

items.f: Moong seeds lie on a wet cloth in the fridge for three days.
items.b: WAIT. They are too cold to germinate. Most wake when they are moved to a shelf.

items.f: A lotus seed lies in wet pond mud. The hard coat has no crack.
items.b: WAIT. The seed is dormant, because water cannot pass the coat.

items.f: A lotus seed about 1,300 years old has a cut filed in the coat and is put in water.
items.b: WAKE. Water reached the embryo, and the embryo was still alive.

items.f: Wheat grains lie in a tomb in Egypt for 3,000 years. Then they get water.
items.b: GONE. Real tomb wheat has never germinated. Too much damage had built up.

items.f: A date seed lies in a dry desert fortress for 2,000 years. Then the seed is soaked and sown.
items.b: WAKE. This happened in 2005. The dry desert air kept the seed alive.

items.f: A mango stone is left to dry on a shelf for two months.
items.b: GONE. A mango seed cannot survive drying, and must be sown fresh.

items.f: Dry paddy seeds are sealed in a packet and kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius for 30 years.
items.b: WAIT. Dry and frozen, the seeds age very slowly.

items.f: Moth mullein seeds lie in a buried bottle of sand for 142 years. Then they are spread on wet soil in the light.
items.b: WAKE. This happened in 2021, in a test begun in 1879.

items.f: Apple seeds from a freshly picked apple are put on a wet cloth in a warm room.
items.b: WAIT. Most apple seeds are dormant until they have had some weeks of cold.

items.f: Tiny lettuce seeds are buried 5 centimetres deep in warm, wet, dark soil.
items.b: WAIT. Many lettuce seeds germinate only after light has reached them.

items.f: Dry moong seeds hang in a closed jar of warm, damp air for a month.
items.b: GONE, for most of them. Seeds take in water from damp air, age fast and grow mould.

items.f: Weed seeds lie deep in garden soil. A gardener digs the bed, and the seeds end up on top in the light and rain.
items.b: WAKE. Light and water tell the seeds they are near the surface.

items.f: Dry tobacco seeds are fixed to the outside of the space station for 18 months. Then they are sown on Earth.
items.b: WAKE, for some of them. This was tested from 2008 to 2009.

items.f: Frozen green peas from a shop packet are put on a wet cloth.
items.b: GONE. The peas were full of water when they were frozen.

items.f: Dry rajma from a kitchen jar are soaked overnight and kept on a wet cloth.
items.b: WAKE. Kitchen rajma are dry, resting seeds, and most are viable.

items.f: Roasted chana are put on a wet cloth.
items.b: GONE. Roasting destroyed the embryo.

items.f: Tamarind seeds with an unbroken hard coat are soaked in water for two days.
items.b: WAIT, for most of them. Water cannot pass the coat until something thins it.

items.f: Jackfruit seeds from a ripe fruit are sown in wet soil the same week.
items.b: WAKE. Jackfruit seeds have no waiting stage, so they must be sown fresh.

printables.title: 3 answer tokens: WAKE, WAIT, GONE. Print one set for each player
items: WAIT: the seed stays alive and does not germinate

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards into a pile, fronts up. Give each player the three answer tokens.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud, keeping the back hidden.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then all the tokens are turned over together.
The reader reads the back. A player whose token matches scores 1 point.
A player who also gives the reason scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's job after every card.
Playing alone? Read the front, say your answer and your reason aloud, and then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right answer.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 24 is your result.

setup.art: A pile of 24 cards on a table and three small tokens marked WAKE, WAIT and GONE in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes three tokens.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another slides a token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. The others put down one token, face down.

setup.art: Tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the answer and the reason.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards. Give each player three tokens.
flow.say: Each card tells what was done to a seed. You decide what happens next: the seed wakes, waits, or is gone.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wake, Wait or Gone. You set up the seed fate cards and the answer tokens.

flow.do: Play the first 12 cards. Read each back aloud. After card 6, ask the question below.
flow.say: Listen to the card. Is there water? Is the seed dry or wet? Has the root come out? Choose your token.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Choose WAKE, WAIT or GONE. Turn your token over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do you ask yourself first, to decide a seed's fate?
good: Is the seed dry or wet?
Has the root come out yet?
Does the seed have water, air and warmth?

flow.parent: For a stuck player, ask three things. Is the embryo still whole? Has the seed got what a seed needs? Is something holding the seed back?
flow.context: In this step of Wake, Wait or Gone you play the first 12 seed fate cards.

flow.do: Play the last 12 cards. Add up the points. Then each player picks the card that surprised them most and says why.
flow.say: Let's finish the pile. Then tell me which card surprised you most.
flow.kid: Play the rest of the cards. Add up your points. Which card surprised you most?

check.q: Which seed is most likely to be alive after 50 years?
options: A dry seed kept in damp air
check.why: Dry and cold together slow a seed's ageing the most. A soaked seed is killed by ice, and damp air ages a seed fast. This is a game moment, so talk about it and play on.

flow.context: This is the last step of Wake, Wait or Gone. You finish the seed fate cards and count the points.

experiments.title: The Freezer Test: can a seed live through a night in the freezer?
experiments.context: In this five-day experiment you put dry moong seeds and soaked moong seeds in the freezer for one night. Then you give all the seeds water and count how many germinate.
experiments.question: Does one night in a freezer kill a moong seed? Does the answer depend on whether the seed is dry or soaked?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. There are four groups of 20 seeds: dry on the shelf, dry in the freezer, soaked on the shelf and soaked in the freezer. How many of each 20 will germinate? Why do you think so? Write your four guesses and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: All 80 seeds come from one packet, and each group has 20. Every group germinates on the same kind of wet cloth, on the same shelf. Two variables are changed: dry or soaked, and shelf or freezer. The four groups test every mix of the two. Group A, dry on the shelf, is the control group. The groups get water at different times, so compare the final counts on day 5 and not the speed.

materials.item: whole green moong seeds from one packet (not split dal), with no cracks or holes
small bowls or katoris: 2 for soaking and keeping seeds, 2 that can go in the freezer
steel plates, and 4 more plates to use as lids
pieces of clean cotton cloth or kitchen tissue, each about the size of a plate
a cup of water, a marker and paper or tape for the labels A, B, C and D
a freezer, and a shelf away from direct sunlight

experiments.safety: Do not eat any seeds from this test. The soaked seeds from the freezer go soft and may smell by day 5. Throw all the seeds away at the end and wash your hands.

schedule.what: In the morning, guess and soak 40 seeds. After 8 hours, put one dry group and one soaked group in the freezer.
Take the two groups out of the freezer. Put all four groups on wet cloths.
Count the seeds with a root in each group. Keep the cloths wet.
Count again.
Make the final count, work out the percentages and draw a bar chart. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 3, 4 and 5. On day 5, turn each count into a percentage. Each seed out of 20 is worth 5 percent. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each group.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seeds germinated by day 5
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be your own.

setup.art: Four small heaps of 20 green moong seeds on a steel plate, with paper labels A, B, C and D.
setup.caption: 1. Count four groups of 20 moong. Soak groups C and D for 8 hours. Keep A and B dry.

setup.art: An open freezer with two small steel bowls inside, one holding dry moong and one holding swollen, soaked moong.
setup.caption: 2. Put B (dry) and D (soaked) in the freezer for one night. Keep A and C on the shelf.

setup.art: Four steel plates in a row, each with a wet cloth and 20 moong seeds, and four more plates beside them as lids.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, put every group on a wet cloth. Cover each plate.

setup.art: A child pointing at seeds with small white roots on a wet cloth and writing numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 4. On days 3, 4 and 5, count the seeds with a root in each group.

flow.do: Show your child the plan: four groups of 20 seeds. Ask for a guess for each group, and the reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Some seeds will spend tonight in the freezer. Some will be dry and some will be soaked first. How many of each 20 will still germinate? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four groups of seeds. Two go in the freezer. Guess how many of each 20 will grow. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the freezer will or will not kill the seeds?
good: Cold kills plants, so the seeds will die.
Dry seeds are hard, so cold cannot hurt them.
Wet things turn to ice, and ice might break the seed.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A guess with a reason is what you need. Many children expect the freezer to kill both groups.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Freezer Test. You guess what a night in the freezer does to dry seeds and to soaked seeds.

flow.do: 1. Count out four groups of 20 seeds. Throw out any cracked seed. 2. Put groups C and D in a bowl with water 2 centimetres above them. 3. Keep groups A and B dry in two katoris. 4. Write down the time.
flow.say: We start in the morning. Groups C and D soak for 8 hours. Groups A and B stay dry. Why do we use 20 seeds in each group, and not 2?
flow.kid: Count four groups of 20 seeds. Soak two groups in water. Keep two groups dry.

ask.q: Why 20 seeds in each group, and not 2?
good: One seed might be dead already.
With 20 seeds, one dead seed changes the result only a little.

flow.wait: Leave the seeds to soak for 8 hours
flow.context: In this step of the Freezer Test you count four groups of 20 moong and start soaking two groups.

flow.do: 1. After 8 hours, drain the water. 2. Put soaked group D in one freezer bowl and dry group B in the other. Put both in the freezer. 3. Put soaked group C on a wet cloth on a plate and cover it. 4. Leave dry group A on the shelf.
flow.say: Look how much the soaked seeds have swollen. Now B and D go into the freezer for the night. A and C stay on the shelf.
flow.kid: Drain the soaked seeds. Put B and D in the freezer. Keep A and C on the shelf.

check.q: In the Freezer Test, why do dry seeds go in the freezer too?
options: To see what cold does to a dry seed
To keep the soaked seeds company
To make the dry seeds wet
check.why: Group B shows what cold alone does to a dry seed. Without group B you could not tell whether cold or water caused a result. If you chose another answer, remember that each group is there to test one thing.

flow.parent: The soaked seeds should be swollen but should not yet show a root. In a very hot room, soak for 6 hours.
flow.wait: Leave B and D in the freezer overnight, for about 12 hours
flow.context: In this step of the Freezer Test you put one dry group and one soaked group in the freezer overnight.

flow.do: 1. Take B and D out of the freezer. Leave them for 30 minutes. 2. Let your child look at D and C side by side, and touch them. 3. Label four plates A, B, C and D. 4. Put each group on a wet cloth on a plate. Group C is already on one. 5. Cover every plate and put all four on one shelf.
flow.say: Look at the two soaked groups. Is anything different about the group from the freezer? Now every group gets a wet cloth. Groups A and B get water later than C. So we will compare the final count, not the speed.
flow.kid: Take B and D out. Wait until they thaw. Look closely. Put every group on a wet cloth. Cover the plates.

ask.q: What do you notice about the soaked seeds from the freezer?
good: They look darker.
They feel softer, or the skin is loose.
They look just the same as the others.

flow.parent: The cloth must be wet all through, with no water lying on the plate. The thawed soaked seeds may look darker and feel softer. Sometimes they look the same.
flow.context: In this step of the Freezer Test you take two groups out of the freezer. Then all four groups go on wet cloths.

flow.do: Day 3. Count the seeds with a white root in each plate. Write the four numbers. Sprinkle water if a cloth is drying.
flow.say: Count every seed that has a white root. Which groups are growing? Is that what you guessed?
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a root on each plate. Write the numbers. Keep the cloths wet.
flow.context: In this step of the Freezer Test you make the first count of seeds with a root.

flow.do: Day 4. Count again and write the numbers. Smell plate D from a distance and note any change.
flow.say: Count again. Have any more seeds woken? What is happening on plate D?
flow.kid: Count again. Write the numbers. Look closely at plate D.
flow.context: In this step of the Freezer Test you count the seeds with a root again, one day later.

flow.do: Day 5. 1. Make the final count. 2. Help your child turn each count into a percentage: count times 5. 3. Draw a bar chart with four bars. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 5. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Each seed out of 20 is worth 5 percent. Work out the four percentages and draw the bars. Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Count for the last time. Each seed is 5 percent. Draw four bars. Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Which two groups show what cold does to a dry seed?
good: A and B. Both are dry, and only B was frozen.

ask.q: Which two groups show what cold does to a soaked seed?
good: C and D. Both were soaked, and only D was frozen.

ask.q: So what killed the seeds in group D: the cold, the water, or both together?
good: Both together. Cold alone did not kill B, and water alone did not kill C.

flow.parent: Usually groups A, B and C germinate almost fully, and group D hardly at all. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason: a soaked seed is full of water. In the freezer the water turns to sharp ice crystals that tear the cells. A dry seed is only about one tenth water, and that water is held too tightly to form ice. So cold does not harm a dry seed. If some group D seeds grew, they may not have frozen right through.
flow.think: A seed bank keeps seeds in freezers. What must the bank do to every seed before freezing?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Freezer Test. You compare how many dry and soaked moong seeds germinated after a night in the freezer.

experiments.title: No Going Back: can a waking seed be dried again?
experiments.context: In this seven-day experiment you soak moong seeds and then dry them again. Some are dried before a root appears and some after. Then you give all of them water and see who grows.
experiments.question: Can a moong seed be dried again after soaking, and still grow later? Does the answer change once the root has come out?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Group A is never wet. Group B is soaked for 6 hours and then dried. Group C is allowed to grow a root and is then dried. When all three get water again, how many of each 20 will grow? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the seeds come from one packet, and each group ends with 20. Groups B and C are dried side by side on the same kind of plate, until both are hard. All three groups get water again on the same day, on the same kind of cloth and shelf. Only one variable is changed: how far the seed had gone before drying. Group A, never wet, is the control group.

materials.item: whole green moong seeds from one packet: 20 for group A, 20 for group B and 25 for group C
a bowl for soaking, and a katori to keep group A dry
steel plates: 2 for drying, 3 for germinating, and 3 to use as lids
pieces of clean cotton cloth or kitchen tissue, each about the size of a plate
a ruler, a marker and paper or tape for the labels A, B and C
a shelf under a fan or near an open window, away from direct sunlight

experiments.safety: Do not eat any seeds from this test. Dried sprouts can grow mould. Throw all the seeds away at the end and wash your hands.

schedule.what: In the morning, guess and soak 45 seeds. After 6 hours, spread group B to dry and put group C on a wet cloth.
When group C has roots about 1 centimetre long, spread 20 of them to dry beside group B.
Check that B and C are hard and dry. Put groups A, B and C on wet cloths.
Count the seeds that are growing in each group.
Make the final count and work out the percentages. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 6 and 7. A seed counts as growing if there is a firm white root at least 2 centimetres long. On day 7, turn each count into a percentage. Draw one seed from each group.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seeds growing on day 7
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be your own.

setup.art: A bowl of moong seeds soaking in water beside a katori of dry moong labelled A, with a clock showing morning.
setup.caption: 1. Soak 45 moong for 6 hours. Keep 20 dry as group A.

setup.art: A dry steel plate with swollen moong spread in one layer under a ceiling fan, labelled B.
setup.caption: 2. Spread 20 soaked seeds on a dry plate. This is group B.

setup.art: A ruler beside moong sprouts with white roots about 1 centimetre long, being moved onto a dry plate labelled C.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, when the others have roots about 1 centimetre long, spread 20 to dry. This is group C.

setup.art: Three covered plates labelled A, B and C on a shelf, with one lid lifted to show seeds on a wet cloth.
setup.caption: 4. On day 4, give all three groups a wet cloth. Count who is growing on days 6 and 7.

flow.do: Explain the three groups. Ask for a guess for each group and the reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Group A stays dry all along. Group B is soaked and dried again. Group C grows a root and is then dried. Later they all get water. How many of each 20 will grow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three groups of seeds. Two will be wetted and dried again. Guess how many will grow later. Say why.

ask.q: Do you think a seed with a root can dry out and wait again? Why?
good: Yes, because seeds are made to be dry.
No, because the root is soft and will die.
Maybe some, if the root is very short.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children expect group B to die too.
flow.context: This is the first step of No Going Back. You guess whether seeds that are soaked and then dried can still grow.

flow.do: 1. Count 20 seeds into a dry katori. This is group A. 2. Put 45 more seeds in a bowl, with water 2 centimetres above them. 3. Write down the time.
flow.say: We start in the morning. Group A stays dry. The other 45 seeds soak for 6 hours.
flow.kid: Count 20 seeds for group A. Keep them dry. Soak 45 more seeds in water.
flow.wait: Leave the seeds to soak for 6 hours
flow.context: In this step of No Going Back you set aside 20 dry moong seeds and start soaking 45 more.

flow.do: 1. After 6 hours, drain the water. 2. Spread 20 soaked seeds in one layer on a dry plate, under a fan. This is group B. 3. Put the other 25 on a wet cloth on a plate and cover it. These will become group C.
flow.say: The seeds have swollen, but no root shows yet. Group B dries now. The rest keep their water and carry on.
flow.kid: Drain the seeds. Spread 20 on a dry plate. Put 25 on a wet cloth and cover them.
flow.parent: Dry the seeds in moving air and shade, not in hot sun. Hot sun could harm them and spoil the test.
flow.wait: Leave until the next day, when most roots are about 1 centimetre long
flow.context: In this step of No Going Back you start drying 20 soaked moong. The other 25 carry on germinating.

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Measure three roots with the ruler. Most should be half to 1 centimetre long. 2. Choose 20 seeds with a root and spread them on the second dry plate. This is group C. 3. Put it beside group B under the fan.
flow.say: Measure a few roots. Now these 20 seedlings go to dry beside group B. What do you think will happen to the roots?
flow.kid: Measure three roots. Spread 20 rooted seeds on a dry plate. Put them beside group B.
flow.wait: Leave B and C to dry for 2 more days
flow.context: In this step of No Going Back you start to dry 20 moong whose roots are about 1 centimetre long.

flow.do: Day 4. 1. Press a seed from B and one from C. Both should be as hard as seeds from the packet. 2. Let your child describe each group. 3. Label three plates A, B and C. 4. Put each group on a wet cloth, cover the plates and put them on one shelf.
flow.say: Describe the seeds in B and in C. How do they differ from group A? Now all three groups get water on the same day.
flow.kid: Press the seeds. Are they hard? Say how B and C look. Put all three groups on wet cloths.

ask.q: How do the dried seeds of group C look now?
good: The roots are thin, brown threads.
The seeds have shrunk and the skins are loose.

flow.parent: In damp weather, drying can take a day longer. If the seeds dent when pressed, wait another day.
flow.context: In this step of No Going Back you check that the dried moong are hard. Then all three groups get water again.

flow.do: Day 6. Count the seeds in each group that have a firm white root at least 2 centimetres long. Write the numbers. Keep the cloths wet.
flow.say: A seed counts as growing if the root is white, firm and at least 2 centimetres long. Count each group.
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a long white root. Write the numbers. Keep the cloths wet.
flow.context: In this step of No Going Back you count how many moong in each group are growing.

flow.do: Day 7. 1. Make the final count. 2. Turn each count into a percentage: count times 5. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 4. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Count once more and work out the percentages. Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Count for the last time. Work out the percentages. Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Group B and group C were both wetted and both dried. What was different?
good: Group C had already grown a root before drying.
Group B was dried before any root came out.

ask.q: A light shower wakes some seeds in a field, and then no rain comes for two weeks. What happens to them?
good: If their roots are out, they dry and die.
Seeds that had not woken yet are still safe.

flow.parent: Usually groups A and B grow almost fully, and B is often a little faster. Group C mostly stays brown and still. Write down what you really found. The reason: for the first hours of soaking, the embryo keeps the sugars and proteins that protect dry cells. Once the root grows, its new cells are large and full of water, and the protection has been taken apart. Those cells die when they dry. A few group C seeds may grow a new root from higher up.
flow.think: A seed cannot undo waking. How might that explain why many wild seeds wait for a heavy rain?
flow.context: This is the last step of No Going Back. You compare seeds dried before the root came out with seeds dried after.

activities.title: Read the Five Jars: what does a germination test show?
activities.context: In this activity you check someone else's germination test. Five jars of 10 moong seeds were kept in five ways for 8 days. The results are made up, but they are typical. You work out what the test shows and where it is not fair.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write a conclusion in two sentences: what moong seeds need to germinate, and what they do not need. Then write one change that would make the test fairer.

example_chart.title: The Five Jars table: made-up results. Seeds with a root, out of 10 moong in each jar
example_chart.show: Five jars of moong seeds, each kept in a different way for 8 days.

setup.art: Five glass jars in a row, each with 10 moong seeds on cloth: one dry, one wet, one inside a fridge, one under a dark box, one filled with water with a shiny layer of oil on top.
setup.caption: 1. Five jars of 10 moong seeds were kept in five ways.

setup.art: A table of numbers with five rows and four columns for days 2, 4, 6 and 8.
setup.caption: 2. Every two days, the seeds with a root were counted.

setup.art: A child pointing at two rows of the table with two fingers, comparing them.
setup.caption: 3. Compare two jars at a time. What is the one difference between them?

flow.do: Look at the Five Jars table together. Ask your child what they notice. Then ask which jar is the control group.
flow.say: Here are five jars of moong, kept in five ways. Read the table. What do you notice? Which jar had the ordinary treatment that the others are compared with?
flow.kid: Read the table of five jars. What do you notice? Which jar is the control?

chart.title: The Five Jars table: made-up results. Seeds with a root, out of 10 moong in each jar
chart.show: Five jars of moong seeds, each kept in a different way for 8 days.

ask.q: Which jar is the control group, and why?
good: Jar 2. It has water, air, warmth and light, and each other jar changes one thing.

flow.parent: Jar 2 is the control: wet cloth, on the shelf, in the light.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Five Jars. You read a table of made-up results from a germination test with five jars.

flow.do: For jars 1, 3, 4 and 5, ask which variable was changed compared with jar 2. Write the four variables: water, warmth, light and air.
flow.say: Compare each jar with jar 2. What one thing is different? What does each pair tell you?
flow.kid: Compare each jar with jar 2. Name the one thing that is different. Write it down.

chart.title: The Five Jars table: made-up results. Seeds with a root, out of 10 moong in each jar
chart.show: Five jars of moong seeds, each kept in a different way for 8 days.

check.q: In the Five Jars table, which two jars test whether moong seeds need light?
check.why: Jars 2 and 4 are both wet and warm, and only the light differs. Jar 4 in the dark germinated fully, so moong do not need light. Jars 1 and 2 differ in water, not light.

flow.parent: The oil in jar 5 stops air from dissolving into the water, so those seeds get almost no oxygen.
flow.context: In this step of Read the Five Jars you find which variable each jar changes, compared with the control jar.

flow.do: Ask about jar 3. A fridge is cold, and it is also dark. Ask whether that is fair, and which other jar helps. Then ask why the test ran for 8 days and not 4.
flow.say: The fridge jar differs from jar 2 in two ways. What are they? Which jar shows that darkness was not the cause? Now look at jar 3 on day 4 and on day 8.
flow.kid: The fridge is cold and dark. Is that fair? Which jar helps you decide? Look at jar 3 on day 8.

chart.title: The Five Jars table: made-up results. Seeds with a root, out of 10 moong in each jar
chart.show: Five jars of moong seeds, each kept in a different way for 8 days.

ask.q: The fridge jar was cold and dark. How do we know the cold slowed the seeds, not the dark?
good: Jar 4 was dark and warm, and all 10 germinated.
So darkness does not stop moong. The cold must be the cause.

ask.q: What would you have said about cold if the test had stopped on day 4?
good: That cold stops seeds completely.
By day 8 two had woken, so cold slows them down a lot.

flow.parent: When two things change at once, you cannot tell which caused the result. Here jar 4 untangles the two.
flow.context: In this step of Read the Five Jars you find a place where the test is not quite fair. You also see why a test must run for many days.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns each day 8 count into a percentage: count times 10. 2. They write a conclusion in two sentences. 3. Ask why each jar had 10 seeds and not 1.
flow.say: Each seed out of 10 is worth 10 percent. Work out the five percentages. Then write what moong need to germinate, and what they do not need.
flow.kid: Work out the percentage for each jar. Write what seeds need. Write what they do not need.

chart.title: The Five Jars table: made-up results. Seeds with a root, out of 10 moong in each jar
chart.show: Five jars of moong seeds, each kept in a different way for 8 days.

ask.q: In jar 2, one seed never germinated. What if jar 2 had held only that one seed?
good: We would have said that wet, warm seeds do not germinate.
One dead seed would have given the wrong answer.

flow.parent: A good conclusion: moong need water, air and warmth to germinate. They do not need light. A fairer test would use more seeds in each jar, or repeat every jar.
flow.context: This is the last step of Read the Five Jars. You write what the five-jar germination test shows.

activities.title: The Rag Doll Test: test 50 seeds the way a seed lab does
activities.context: In this activity you roll 50 seeds in a wet cloth and count the strong seedlings four days later. Farmers call this the rag doll test. It tells you the germination percentage of a packet before you sow.

materials.item: seeds from the oldest packet of whole seeds in your home: moong, methi, lobia, chana or leftover garden seeds
a clean cotton cloth about 30 centimetres square, such as an old handkerchief
thread or 2 rubber bands, a tall tumbler and a plate or plastic bag to cover it
a ruler, a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Do not eat the test seeds. Wash your hands after sorting them.

schedule.what: Guess. Lay 50 seeds in rows on a wet cloth, roll the cloth up and stand the roll in a tumbler.
Unroll the cloth. Sort the seeds into strong seedlings, weak seedlings and seeds that did not wake. Work out the percentage.

activities.record: Write three numbers: strong seedlings, weak seedlings and seeds that did not wake. They must add up to 50. Write the germination percentage, which is the number of strong seedlings times 2.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for 50 old moong seeds

setup.art: A wet square cloth on a table with 50 seeds laid in five neat rows of ten across the upper half.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 50 seeds in 5 rows of 10 on a wet cloth.

setup.art: Hands folding the lower half of the cloth over the seeds and rolling the cloth loosely like a mat.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the cloth over the seeds and roll it up loosely.

setup.art: A rolled cloth tied at both ends, standing upright in a steel tumbler with a plate on top.
setup.caption: 3. Tie the roll, stand it in a tumbler and cover it.

setup.art: An unrolled cloth with three heaps: long white seedlings, short brown ones and seeds with no root.
setup.caption: 4. On day 4, unroll and sort the seeds into three heaps.

flow.do: Show your child the packet. Ask how many of 50 seeds they think will grow into strong seedlings, and why. Write the guess.
flow.say: This is our oldest packet. Out of 50 seeds, how many will grow into strong seedlings? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the old packet. Guess how many of 50 will grow well. Say why.
flow.parent: Stir the packet first and take the 50 seeds without choosing. Picking the best-looking seeds would make the result too high.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rag Doll Test. You guess how many seeds from an old packet are still able to grow.

flow.do: 1. Wet the cloth and wring it out. 2. Lay 50 seeds in 5 rows of 10 on the upper half. 3. Fold the lower half over the seeds. 4. Roll the cloth loosely and tie both ends. 5. Stand the roll in a tumbler and cover it. 6. Sprinkle water on the roll once a day.
flow.say: Rows of ten make the seeds easy to count later. Roll the cloth loosely, so that air can reach the seeds.
flow.kid: Wet the cloth. Lay 50 seeds in rows of 10. Fold, roll and tie. Stand the roll in a tumbler.

ask.q: Why must the roll be loose and only damp, not soaking?
good: Seeds need air as well as water.
Seeds sitting in water get too little oxygen.

flow.wait: Leave the roll for 3 days, sprinkling water once a day
flow.context: In this step of the Rag Doll Test you roll 50 seeds in a wet cloth so they can germinate.

flow.do: Day 4. 1. Unroll the cloth. 2. Sort the seeds into three heaps. Strong: a firm white root at least 2 centimetres long. Weak: a short, brown or broken root, or mould. Did not wake: no root. 3. Count each heap.
flow.say: A seed lab counts only strong seedlings, because a weak one may die in a field. Sort yours into strong, weak and not woken. Do the three numbers add up to 50?
flow.kid: Unroll the cloth. Make three heaps: strong, weak, not woken. Count each heap.
flow.parent: Chana and lobia are slower. Give them one more day before you sort.
flow.context: In this step of the Rag Doll Test you unroll the cloth and sort the 50 seeds into three heaps.

flow.do: 1. Double the number of strong seedlings to get the percentage. 2. Compare it with 75 percent, the lowest allowed on a certified moong packet in India. 3. Work out how many seeds to sow for 20 plants.
flow.say: 50 seeds is half of 100, so double your number of strong seedlings. Is your packet above 75 percent? How many seeds would you sow to get 20 plants?
flow.kid: Double the strong seedlings. That is your percentage. How many seeds would you sow for 20 plants?

ask.q: Your packet scores 80 percent. How many seeds should you sow to get 20 plants?
good: 25 seeds. 80 percent of 25 is 20.
More than 20, because 2 in every 10 will fail.

flow.parent: If the packet scores far below 75 percent, sow extra seeds or buy fresh ones. The unwoken seeds may be dead, or a few may be dormant.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Rag Doll Test. You turn your count of strong seedlings into a germination percentage.

activities.title: Four Days, Four Drawings: what happens inside a waking chana?
activities.context: In this activity you open one chana each day for four days, from dry seed to seedling. You draw and label what you find, and put the steps of germination in order.

materials.item: kabuli chana (the big pale kind), whole and uncooked
a bowl of water, a steel plate with a lid and a piece of cotton cloth
a ruler, a notebook, a pencil and a hand lens or a phone camera to zoom in

activities.safety: Do not eat the chana you have handled and opened.

schedule.what: Draw a dry chana and measure it. Soak 7 chana overnight.
Measure a soaked chana, open the chana and draw the three parts. Put the other 6 on a wet cloth.
Open one chana and draw what has changed.
Open one more chana, draw it, and write the steps of germination in order.

activities.record: Make four drawings, one for each day, with the day written under each. Label the seed coat, the food store (cotyledons), the radicle and the plumule. Write the length of the chana or of the root beside each drawing.

setup.art: A dry kabuli chana beside a ruler, with its small pointed beak facing right.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: draw and measure a dry chana. Soak 7 overnight.

setup.art: A soaked chana opened into two pale halves, with a tiny pointed plant at one end.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: open a soaked chana. Find the tiny plant between the two halves.

setup.art: Six chana on a wet cloth on a steel plate, some with short white roots.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the others on a wet cloth. Open one each day.

setup.art: A notebook page with four labelled drawings in a row, from dry seed to seedling.
setup.caption: 4. Draw what you find each day, and label the parts.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a dry chana and finds the small pointed beak. 2. They measure the length with a ruler. 3. Soak 7 chana in a bowl overnight. Keep 1 dry.
flow.say: Look closely at a dry chana. Find the small beak at one end. What do you think lies under that beak? Draw the chana and measure it.
flow.kid: Draw a dry chana. Find the small beak. Measure the chana. Soak 7 overnight.

ask.q: What do you think is under the beak of the chana?
good: The part that will grow.
The baby plant's root.

flow.wait: Leave the chana to soak overnight
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Days, Four Drawings. You draw and measure a dry chana before any water reaches the seed.

flow.do: 1. Put a soaked chana beside the dry one and measure both. 2. Peel the skin off the soaked chana. 3. Open the two halves gently with a thumbnail. 4. Find the tiny plant at the beak end. 5. Your child draws and labels the parts. 6. Put the other 6 soaked chana on a wet cloth and cover them.
flow.say: How much longer is the soaked chana? Now peel the skin and open the two halves. Find the tiny plant. Which end points out, and which end is tucked inside?
flow.kid: Measure the soaked chana. Peel the skin. Open the halves. Find the tiny plant. Draw and label.

check.q: In a soaked chana, what are the two big halves?
options: The food store for the young plant
check.why: The two halves are the cotyledons, which hold the food. The young plant is the tiny pointed part joined to them. If you chose two plants, look again: there is only one tiny root.

flow.parent: The skin is the seed coat. The halves are the cotyledons. The pointed tip under the beak is the radicle, and the tiny folded tip between the halves is the plumule.
flow.context: In this step of Four Days, Four Drawings you open a soaked chana. You find the seed coat, the food store and the embryo.

flow.do: Day 3. Look at the chana on the cloth. Most have a white root coming out near the beak. Open one, measure the root and draw it.
flow.say: What came out first, and from where? Measure the root. Is the shoot showing yet?
flow.kid: Look at the chana on the cloth. What came out first? Open one. Measure the root. Draw.

ask.q: Which came out first, the root or the shoot? Why might that order help the seedling?
good: The root. The seedling needs water before anything else.
The root also holds the seedling in place.

flow.context: In this step of Four Days, Four Drawings you see which part of the chana embryo comes out first.

flow.do: Day 4. 1. Open one more chana and draw it. 2. Look between the halves for the plumule, which is now longer. 3. Your child writes the steps of germination in order under the four drawings.
flow.say: Find the plumule between the halves. Has it grown? Now write, in order, everything that has happened to a chana since day 1.
flow.kid: Open one more chana. Find the tiny shoot. Draw it. Write the steps in order.

ask.q: Say the steps of germination in order.
good: The seed takes in water and swells.
The seed coat splits.
The radicle comes out and grows down.
The plumule grows up, and then the first leaves open.

flow.parent: The first two halves often look a little thinner by day 4. The embryo is using the food. You can plant the remaining chana in a pot.
flow.context: This is the last step of Four Days, Four Drawings. You put the steps of germination in order from your own four drawings.

projects.title: Three Jars, Three Weeks: what makes stored seeds die?
projects.context: In this project you store moong seeds in three closed jars for three weeks: dry on a shelf, dry in the fridge, and in damp air on a shelf. Each week you test 20 seeds from each jar.

materials.item: whole green moong seeds from one packet: 70 for each jar and 20 for the first test (about one heaped tablespoon)
clean, dry glass jars with tight lids, such as jam or pickle jars
squares of thin cotton cloth, about 12 centimetres across, and 3 pieces of thread about 20 centimetres long
tablespoons of water, for the damp jar only
steel plates with lids and pieces of cloth for the germination tests
a marker and labels: Dry shelf, Dry fridge, Damp shelf
squared paper or a notebook page for a line graph

projects.safety: The seeds in the damp jar are likely to grow mould. A grown-up opens that jar, near an open window. Do not smell it closely. Wash hands after every test. A child with asthma or a dust allergy should watch from a distance. Throw all the seeds away at the end.

schedule.what: Set up the three jars. Put 20 seeds from the packet on a wet cloth as the first test.
Count how many of the first 20 seeds germinated.
Week 1: take 20 seeds from each jar and put them on wet cloths.
Count the week 1 seeds with a root.
Week 2: take 20 seeds from each jar and put them on wet cloths.
Count the week 2 seeds with a root.
Week 3: take 20 seeds from each jar and put them on wet cloths.
Count the week 3 seeds. Draw a line graph for each jar. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.

projects.record: Make a table with a row for each jar. The columns are the start, week 1, week 2 and week 3. Write the number germinated out of 20 and the percentage. Draw a line graph with weeks along the bottom and percent germinated up the side, one line for each jar.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: percent of 20 seeds that germinated

setup.art: Three glass jars with lids, each with a small cloth pouch of seeds hanging inside from a thread held by the lid. One jar has a little water at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a pouch of 70 moong in each jar. Add 3 tablespoons of water to the damp jar only.

setup.art: One jar on a fridge shelf and two jars on a kitchen shelf, with labels Dry fridge, Dry shelf and Damp shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Put one dry jar in the fridge. Keep the other dry jar and the damp jar on a shelf.

setup.art: Three plates with wet cloths and 20 seeds each, labelled with the jar names and 'Week 1'.
setup.caption: 3. Each week, test 20 seeds from each jar on a wet cloth.

setup.art: A hand-drawn line graph with three lines, two staying high and one falling week by week.
setup.caption: 4. After three weeks, draw a line for each jar.

flow.do: 1. Tie 70 seeds loosely in each cloth square to make three pouches. 2. Hang one pouch inside each jar by a thread, and trap the thread under the lid. 3. Pour 3 tablespoons of water into the bottom of one jar. The pouch must hang above the water. 4. Label the jars and close them tightly. 5. Put the Dry fridge jar in the fridge and the other two on a shelf. 6. Put 20 seeds from the packet on a wet cloth, as the first test.
flow.say: Seed banks keep seeds dry and cold. We will test what happens when seeds are kept dry, dry and cold, or damp. Which jar of seeds will stay alive best for three weeks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make three seed pouches. Hang one in each jar. Add water to one jar only. Guess which seeds stay alive best. Say why.

ask.q: The seeds in the damp jar never touch the water. Can the water still reach them? How?
good: Yes, as water vapour in the air of the jar.
The air in the jar becomes damp, and the seeds take in the damp.

flow.parent: The seeds in the damp jar must not get wet, only sit in damp air. Keep both shelf jars out of the sun.
flow.wait: Leave the jars closed for one week
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Jars, Three Weeks. You set up three jars of moong seeds: dry on a shelf, dry in the fridge, and damp on a shelf.

flow.do: Day 4. Count how many of the first 20 seeds have a root. Work out the percentage. This is the starting number for all three jars.
flow.say: This number tells us how good the seeds were at the start. Why do we need it?
flow.kid: Count the first 20 seeds. How many have a root? Work out the percentage.

ask.q: Why do we test the seeds before storing them?
good: So we know how many were alive at the start.
Then we can see how much each jar has changed.

flow.context: In this step of Three Jars, Three Weeks you find the germination percentage of the moong before any storage.

flow.do: Day 8. 1. Take the fridge jar out and leave it closed for 30 minutes. 2. A grown-up opens each jar in turn, lifts out the pouch and counts out 20 seeds. 3. Hang the pouch back and close the jar. 4. Put each 20 on a wet cloth on a labelled plate. Cover the plates.
flow.say: A cold jar must warm up before we open it. Otherwise damp from the air settles on the cold seeds. Look at the seeds from each jar. Do they look or feel different?
flow.kid: A grown-up opens the jars. Count 20 seeds from each. Put them on wet cloths. Label each plate.
flow.parent: Seeds from the damp jar may look dull, feel softer or show a little fuzz. If you see roots in the pouch, drops of water fell on the seeds. Write that down too.
flow.wait: Count the seeds with a root 3 days later
flow.context: In this step of Three Jars, Three Weeks you take 20 moong from each jar after one week. You start a germination test.

flow.do: Day 11. Count the seeds with a root on each plate. Write the numbers and the percentages in the table.
flow.say: Count each plate. Is any jar different from the start yet?
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a root. Write the three numbers.
flow.context: In this step of Three Jars, Three Weeks you count how many moong germinated after one week in each jar.

flow.do: Days 15 and 22. Repeat the test each week: 20 seeds from each jar onto wet cloths. Count them 3 days later, on days 18 and 25. Each test takes about 10 minutes and each count about 5 minutes.
flow.say: We do the same test in week 2 and week 3. Keep everything the same each time. What do you expect to change?
flow.kid: Test 20 seeds from each jar again. Do this in week 2 and week 3. Count after 3 days.
flow.context: In this step of Three Jars, Three Weeks you repeat the germination test after two weeks and after three weeks.

flow.do: Day 25. 1. Help your child draw a line graph with three lines. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Draw one line for each jar. Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Did the fridge make a difference in three weeks?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each jar. Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Which did more harm in three weeks: warmth or damp?
good: Damp. The dry shelf jar stayed about the same.
The seeds in damp air died, even though they were never wet.

ask.q: The two dry jars look the same after three weeks. Does that prove cold does not help?
good: No. Three weeks may be too short to show it.
Seed banks see the difference over many years.

flow.parent: Usually the two dry jars stay near the starting number, and the damp jar falls week by week. In a cool room the fall is slower, so add a fourth and fifth week. The reason: seeds take in water from damp air. With more water inside, the glassy state softens and the seed's chemistry speeds up. Damage builds up fast, and moulds grow on the seeds. Cold slows the same damage. Three weeks is too short to show that with dry seeds.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Jars, Three Weeks. You compare how well moong stayed alive in dry, cold and damp storage.

challenges.title: The Power Cut: keep a frozen sample frozen without a freezer
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A seed bank must stay frozen even when the electricity fails. Here an ice cube stands for a frozen packet of seeds. You design a holder that keeps the cube frozen.
challenges.problem: The power has failed at your seed bank. One ice cube is your frozen seed sample. Build a holder from things at home that keeps the cube from melting for as long as possible. Test it against a bare cube in an open katori. After 90 minutes, your holder must have less meltwater than the bare cube.
constraints: Use ice cubes of the same size from the same tray, taken out at the same moment.
No fridge, no freezer and no extra ice.
The holder must fit inside a shoebox.
You must be able to take the cube out to check it in under 10 seconds.
Keep both cubes in the same room, out of the sun.
materials: 3 ice cubes of the same size
a teaspoon, to measure the meltwater
newspaper, an old towel or a woollen cap
a steel dabba or a plastic box with a lid
cotton wool, dry sand or dry soil in a pot, if you have some
general: Wrap the katori in several layers of newspaper.
Put the katori inside a closed dabba, and wrap the dabba in a towel.
Fill the gaps around the katori with cotton wool or crumpled paper.
creative: Put a small box inside a bigger box, with a layer of still air or crumpled paper between them.
Bury the closed dabba in a pot of dry sand or soil. The Svalbard seed vault is dug into frozen rock in the same way.
Chill the empty holder in the fridge before the test starts, so the holder does not warm the cube.
Find the coolest spot in your home: on the floor, away from windows and the kitchen.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own holder. Draw it and build it. Test it beside a bare cube for 90 minutes, and measure the meltwater from each in teaspoons. Then change one thing and test again. Write which change helped most.

flow.say: Heat from the warm room flows into the cold cube. Your holder must slow that heat down. What will you use, and why?
flow.kid: Read the problem. What melts the ice? Draw your plan to slow the heat.

good: From the warm air of the room.
From the table and the katori, and from hands.

good: The rock around it stays below freezing all year.
If the cooling machines stop, the seeds still stay frozen.

flow.parent: The rock at Svalbard is permafrost, which is ground that stays frozen all year. Machines cool the vault further, to minus 18 degrees Celsius. Praise a clear account of what changed and why.

items.p: Which part of a seed is the young plant?
items.why: The embryo is the young plant, with a tiny root and a tiny shoot. The seed coat protects the embryo, and the food store feeds the embryo.

items.p: Put the steps of germination in order.
items: The seed takes in water and swells
The radicle grows out and turns down
a: The seed takes in water and swells
The radicle grows out and turns down
items.why: Water must go in first. Then the coat splits and the root comes out before the shoot. The leaves open last and start to make food.

items.p: Label four parts on this picture of an opened bean seed: seed coat, cotyledon, radicle, plumule.
a: Seed coat: the thin skin around the outside
Cotyledon: one of the two thick halves, which hold the food
Radicle: the tiny pointed root at the edge
Plumule: the tiny folded shoot between the halves
items.why: The seed coat protects, the cotyledons feed, and the radicle and plumule are the two ends of the embryo.
items.art: An opened bean seed showing the skin, the two thick halves and a tiny plant with a pointed root and a folded shoot, with four blank label lines.

items.p: The first root that comes out of a seed is called the ____.
items.why: The radicle is the embryo's root. It always comes out before the shoot, so the seedling can take in water.

items.p: A moong seed needs light to germinate.
items.why: False. Moong germinate in a dark cupboard, because the embryo lives on the food store. A few kinds of seed, such as lettuce, do need light.

items.p: To test whether seeds need water, which two jars should you compare?
opts: Wet warm jar and dry warm jar
Wet warm jar and wet cold jar
Dry warm jar and wet cold jar
items.why: Only the water should differ between the two jars. If warmth changed too, you could not tell which one caused the result.

items.p: Sort these. Do most seeds need each one to germinate?
items.a: see items
items.why: Seeds germinate on a wet cloth in a dark cupboard, so they need neither soil nor light. Without water, air or warmth they do not germinate.

items.p: 18 of 20 seeds germinate. Each seed is worth 5 percent. What is the germination percentage?
items.why: 18 times 5 is 90. So 90 out of every 100 seeds would germinate.

items.p: A germination test uses 20 seeds in each group, not 1. Explain why.
items.a: In any batch a few seeds are dead already. With 1 seed, a dead one would give the wrong answer. With 20 seeds, one dead seed changes the result by only 5 percent.
items.why: A strong answer says that single seeds can be dead or odd, and that many seeds make the result steadier.

items.p: What happens inside a soaked seed in a freezer?
items.why: A soaked seed is full of water. The water freezes into sharp crystals that tear the cell membranes, and the cells die.

items.p: Dry moong seeds die after one night in a freezer.
items.why: False. A dry seed holds too little water to form ice, so the cold does no harm. Seed banks store dry seeds in freezers.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: A few seeds tested from a big batch
The group with the ordinary treatment
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A viable seed can germinate. A dormant seed is viable but waiting. A sample stands for the whole batch, and the control is what the other groups are compared with.

items.p: A seed with a root 1 centimetre long is dried for two days. What happens, and why?
items.a: The seedling dies. The new cells of the root are full of water and have lost the protection that dry seeds have. When they dry, they collapse.
items.why: A strong answer says that the root marks a point of no return, and gives the reason: the growing cells can no longer survive drying.

items.p: A seed bank stores dry seeds at about minus ____ degrees Celsius.
items.why: Minus 18 degrees Celsius is about the cold of a home freezer. Cold slows the ageing of a dry seed.

items.p: Where are old crop seeds safest?

views.who: A scientist at a frozen seed bank
views.says: In a freezer. Dry, frozen seeds stay alive for a hundred years, safe from floods and pests.

views.who: A farmer who saves her own seeds
views.says: In my field. Seeds that are sown every year keep up with new pests and new weather.
In both. If my field fails in a bad year, I need a copy kept somewhere else.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about seeds. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. For the freezer: dry, cold seeds age very slowly. For the field: frozen seeds do not adapt, and some seeds cannot be dried. For both: each covers the other's risk.
items.why: Each view is partly right. A strong answer uses a fact about seeds, such as slow ageing in the cold. A strong answer also replies fairly to another view.

items.p: In the Freezer Test, dry seeds germinated equally well from the freezer and from the shelf. What does this show?
items.a: It shows that cold alone does not kill a dry seed. The two groups differ only in the freezer, and the result is the same.
items.why: A strong answer names the one difference between the groups and says that this difference did not change the result.

items.p: Soaked seeds on a shelf: 100 percent. Soaked, frozen: 0 percent. Dry, frozen: 90 percent. What killed the seeds?
items.why: Dry frozen seeds lived, so cold alone is not the cause. Soaked seeds on the shelf lived, so water alone is not the cause. Only the group with both died.

items.p: A dormant seed is a dead seed.
items.why: False. A dormant seed is alive and can germinate later. A dead seed can never germinate.

items.p: A jar in the fridge is cold and also dark. Why is that a problem in a fair test?
items.a: Two variables change at once. If the seeds do not germinate, you cannot tell whether the cold or the dark was the cause. A dark, warm jar is needed to check.
items.why: A strong answer says that only one variable should change, and suggests a way to separate the two.

items.p: A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results is called an ____ result.
items.why: Scientists keep anomalous results in the table and repeat the test. An odd result can be a mistake, or the start of a discovery.

items.p: 41 of 50 seeds grow into strong seedlings. What is the germination percentage?
items.why: 50 is half of 100, so double the count. 41 times 2 is 82 percent.

items.p: A packet tests at 80 percent. How many seeds should you sow to get 40 plants?
items.why: 80 percent means 8 of every 10 seeds grow. To get 40 plants you need 5 lots of 10 seeds, which is 50 seeds.

items.p: Sort these seeds. Can each be dried and stored for years, or must each be sown fresh?
items.a: see items
items.why: Moong, wheat and paddy dry out as they ripen and can wait for years. Mango and jackfruit seeds die if they dry, so they cannot be kept in a frozen seed bank.

items.p: Put the steps of a seed bank in order.
items: Collect the seeds and note the place and date
Clean the seeds and test a sample
Test a sample every few years
a: Collect the seeds and note the place and date
Clean the seeds and test a sample
Test a sample every few years
items.why: Seeds must be dry before they are sealed and frozen, or ice would kill them. Testing goes on for as long as the seeds are stored.

items.p: Why does a seed bank let a cold packet warm up before opening the packet?
items.a: Damp from the room air settles as water on anything cold. If the packet were opened cold, the dry seeds would take in that water. Wetter seeds age faster.
items.why: A strong answer links the cold surface to damp settling on the seeds, and damp to faster ageing.

items.p: Why does a seed bank regrow a sample when germination falls below 85 percent?
opts: Fresh seeds replace the ageing ones
The freezer has become too full
items.why: Stored seeds slowly die, even when frozen. Sowing them while most are still alive gives fresh seeds of the same variety to store again.

items.p: Draw a soaked cell and a dry cell in a freezer. Show what the ice does in each.
items.a: The soaked cell is full of water, with sharp ice crystals poking through the thin skin of the cell. The dry cell is small and solid, with no crystals and an unbroken skin.
items.why: A strong drawing shows ice only where there is water, and shows the damage as torn cell skins.
items.art: Two blank circles side by side under a snowflake, one labelled soaked cell and one labelled dry cell.

items.p: Seeds soaked for a few hours and then dried can still germinate later.
items.why: True. Before the root comes out, the embryo still has the protection of a dry seed. Farmers use this to make seeds come up faster.

items.p: Match each cause to its effect on a stored seed.
pairs: The seed takes in water and ages fast
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Water speeds up the damage inside a seed, and cold slows the damage down. But cold with water inside the seed makes ice, which kills.

items.p: Is a dry seed in a jar alive?

views.says: Not at this moment. Living means feeding, respiring and growing, and the dry seed does none of these.
Yes. The seed keeps every part needed for life in working order. A dead seed does not.
I call a seed alive if the seed grows when I sow. Until then I cannot know.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about dry seeds. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason: a dry seed shows almost no activity. Another: a dry seed germinates with water and a boiled seed never does, so something is kept in the dry seed.
items.why: This is a real disagreement among scientists. A strong answer uses a fact, such as the difference between a dry seed and a boiled seed. A strong answer also replies fairly to another view.

items.p: Plan a fair test of warm and cool soaking water. Say what you change, measure and keep the same.
items.a: Change: the warmth of the soaking water. Measure: how many seeds have a root at each count. Keep the same: the kind and number of seeds, the soaking time, the cloth and the shelf.
items.why: A strong plan changes only one variable and measures something that can be counted. A strong plan also uses many seeds and lists three things kept the same.

items.p: A test finds that 2 of 2 seeds germinated: '100 percent'. Give two reasons not to trust this number.
items.a: Two seeds are too few: one dead seed would have made the result 50 percent. The two seeds may also not stand for the whole batch.
items.why: A strong answer says that a small sample swings widely by chance. A sample must be big enough to stand for the batch.

items.p: Two groups of 20 seeds score 95 percent and 90 percent. What is the fairest conclusion?
opts: No clear difference: it is one seed
The first group is clearly better
items.why: With 20 seeds, 5 percent is a single seed. One seed more or less can happen by chance, so the two groups are about the same.

items.p: Frozen shop peas do not grow. Dry peas from a jar do. Explain why, using water and ice.
items.a: The shop peas were full of water when they were frozen, so ice crystals tore their cells. The dry peas hold too little water to make ice, so their embryos are unharmed.
items.why: A strong answer says that freezing harms only when there is water inside to form ice.

items.p: In the Freezer Test, cold alone killed the soaked seeds.
items.why: False. Dry seeds in the same freezer lived, so cold alone does not kill. The soaked seeds died because cold and water were together.

items.p: A light shower wakes half the seeds in a field. Then no rain comes. Predict what happens to each half.
items.a: The half that woke grow roots and then dry out and die, because a seedling cannot go back to waiting. The half that stayed dormant are still alive and can wake at the next rain.
items.why: A strong answer uses the point of no return, and sees that the seeds that waited save the plant's chances.

items.p: Why is waiting for a heavy rain safer for a desert seed than waking at the first drops?
opts: A woken seedling cannot go back to waiting
Heavy rain is warmer than light rain
Light rain washes the seeds away
items.why: Germination cannot be undone. After a light shower the soil soon dries, and a seedling dies. A heavy rain wets the soil for long enough for roots to grow deep.

items.p: All the living seeds lying in the soil of a place are called the soil seed ____.
items.why: The soil seed bank is why weeds appear in bare soil where nobody sowed anything. Some of its seeds wait for many years.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one make a stored seed live longer, or die sooner?
items: a cold packet opened in damp air
items.a: see items
items.why: Water and warmth speed up the slow damage inside a seed. Dry, cold and sealed storage slows it.

items.p: A seed bank holds 600 seeds of one variety. Each test uses 50. How many tests can the bank do?
items.why: 600 divided by 50 is 12. So a bank cannot test too often, and must regrow the variety before the seeds run out.

items.p: A seed vault is sealed and never opened or tested for 200 years. What might people find inside? Why?
items.a: Some kinds of seed may still be alive, and others will be dead. Even frozen seeds age slowly, and some kinds last only a few decades. With no tests, nobody regrew them in time.
items.why: A strong answer says that freezing slows ageing but does not stop ageing. Testing and regrowing are part of keeping seeds.

items.p: Three of these seeds stay alive when they are dried. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Moong, paddy and wheat dry out as they ripen and can be stored. A mango seed dies if dried, so the stone must be sown fresh.

items.p: People once said that wheat from a 3,000-year-old tomb had grown. Is the claim true?

views.says: Yes. I sowed grain that came from a tomb, and wheat came up.
Not yet. I want proof that the grain truly came from the tomb. I also want a test of many grains that others can watch.

views.who: A child who has read about the lotus
views.says: It could be true. A lotus seed lived for 1,300 years, so old seeds can live.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would settle the question? Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: The botanist's demand is the strongest. Evidence that would settle it: the age of the grain measured by carbon dating, and a watched germination test on many grains. Real tomb grain has failed such tests.
items.why: A strong answer separates what could be true from what has been shown, and names evidence that anyone could check.

items.p: Draw the line graph you expect: percent germinated over 4 weeks, in a dry jar and in a damp jar.
items.a: Two lines that start at the same high point. The dry jar line stays nearly flat. The damp jar line falls, slowly at first and then faster.
items.why: A strong graph has weeks along the bottom and percent up the side. Both lines start together, and only the damp line falls.
items.art: Blank graph axes with weeks 0 to 4 along the bottom and 0 to 100 percent up the side.

items.p: Match each test result to what it most likely means.
pairs: No seeds germinate, even in the control
The seeds were dead, or the test went wrong
The changed variable does not matter here
One group is far below the control
The change harmed or stopped the seeds
A few seeds wake days after the rest
Seeds in a batch wake at different times
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The control group tells you whether the seeds and the test were sound. Only then can a difference between groups be trusted.

quiz.p: What comes out of a germinating seed first?
quiz.why: The root, called the radicle, comes out first and turns down. The seedling needs water and a hold on the ground before anything else.

quiz.p: What feeds a seedling before the first green leaves open?
opts: The food store in the seed
quiz.why: The embryo lives on the food the parent plant packed into the seed. That is why a seed can germinate in the dark.

quiz.p: Which three things do most seeds need to germinate?
quiz.why: Fair tests show that seeds without water, air or warmth do not germinate. Most germinate without light or soil.

quiz.p: Seeds in a dark box germinate as well as seeds in the light. What does this show?
opts: These seeds do not need light
quiz.why: The two groups differ only in light, and the result is the same. So light does not matter for these seeds.

quiz.p: 9 of 10 seeds germinate. What is the germination percentage?
quiz.why: Each seed out of 10 is worth 10 percent, and 9 times 10 is 90.

quiz.p: A test with 5 seeds gives a steadier answer than a test with 100 seeds.
quiz.why: False. With 5 seeds, one dead seed changes the result by 20 percent. With 100 seeds, one dead seed changes the result by 1 percent.

quiz.p: Why does a dry seed live through a night in a freezer?
opts: Too little water inside to form ice
The seed coat keeps the cold out
A dry seed is already dead
The seed grows a thicker coat
quiz.why: Freezing harms cells when the water in them turns to ice. A dry seed is only about one tenth water, held too tightly to freeze into crystals.

quiz.p: Soaked seeds are frozen, thawed and put on a wet cloth. What is most likely?
quiz.why: Ice crystals formed inside the wet cells and tore them. The cells leak and die when they thaw.

quiz.p: When can a soaked seed still be dried again safely?
quiz.why: For the first hours the embryo keeps the protection of a dry seed. Once the root grows, the new cells cannot survive drying.

opts: A living seed that is not germinating
quiz.why: A dormant seed is alive and waiting. Some dormant seeds wait even when they have water, warmth and air.

quiz.p: How does a seed bank keep seeds alive for decades?
quiz.why: Dry seeds age slowly, and cold slows them further. Sealing keeps damp air out. Soaked seeds would be killed by ice.

quiz.p: What can a farmer's field do for a crop variety that a freezer cannot?
opts: Keep the seeds safe from floods
Hold thousands of varieties in one room
quiz.why: Seeds sown every year face each year's weather and pests, and the plants that do well leave the most seed. A frozen seed stays as the seed was.

applications: Seed packets in India print the germination percentage and the date of the test. A farmer uses the number to decide how much seed to sow.
Seed banks dry seeds and freeze them at about minus 18 degrees Celsius. India's National Genebank in New Delhi keeps more than 4 lakh samples this way.
Many farmers soak seeds overnight and dry the surface before sowing. The seeds come up faster. This works because a seed can be dried again before the root appears.
Families store grain and seed with dried neem leaves in sealed pots, tins and bins. Keeping the seeds dry matters most.
When a flood, a drought or a war wipes out a crop variety, a seed bank can send seeds back. Scientists from Aleppo in Syria rebuilt their collection this way from 2015.
Plant breeders search seed banks for old varieties that stand salt, heat or disease, and cross them with today's crops.
Gardeners who turn over the soil soon see weeds, because digging brings buried seeds up to the light.

open_questions.q: What is the longest time a seed can stay alive?
open_questions.why_open: The record so far is about 2,000 years, for a date palm seed. Nobody knows the limit, and tests like the buried bottles take centuries.

open_questions.q: Is anything at all happening inside a very dry, frozen seed?
open_questions.why_open: Any activity is too small to measure with today's tools. So nobody can say whether the seed's chemistry is very slow or fully stopped.

open_questions.q: How does a waking seed repair damage that built up over many years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists see repair of DNA in the first hours after water enters. They do not yet know how much damage a seed can repair, or why repair finally fails.

open_questions.q: Why do some seeds live for centuries and others for only a few years, even in the same freezer?
open_questions.why_open: Oily seeds often age faster, but that does not explain all the differences. Seed banks are still collecting the data.

open_questions.q: How can seeds that die when dried, such as mango and jackfruit, be stored for a long time?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can freeze the tiny embryos of a few kinds in liquid nitrogen. For most kinds, no method works well yet.

open_questions.q: Will seeds frozen today still suit the weather and pests of a hundred years from now?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody knows how fast the climate and pests will change. Nobody knows how well an old variety will cope when sown again.

ask_kids: Which dry seeds in our kitchen do you think are alive right now? How could we find out without using them all up?

If we could save the seeds of only five plants for the future, which five would you choose?
