jokes.a: There was no water inside to get cold feet.

jokes.j: What did the seed bank say to the new seed?
jokes.a: Stay cool and stay dry. We will call you in ten years.

jokes.j: Why did the sprout refuse to go back in the jar?
jokes.a: The root was out, and there was no going back.

jokes.j: How do you know a seed is patient?
jokes.a: One waited 2,000 years and did not complain once.

jokes.j: Why did the scientist test a hundred seeds and not one?
jokes.a: One seed can be lazy. A hundred cannot all be.

jokes.j: What did the lotus seed say after 1,300 years?
Why did the soaked seed fail the freezer test?
jokes.a: The ice was too sharp for a soft seed.

jokes.j: What is a seed's favourite game?
Why do weeds love a gardener who digs?
jokes.a: Every turn of the spade is a wake-up call.

maths.problem: In the Freezer Test, 19 of 20 dry seeds from the shelf germinated. From the freezer, 18 of 20 dry seeds germinated. What is each percentage? Is the difference big enough to matter?
maths.answer: 95 percent and 90 percent. The difference is too small to matter.
maths.explain: Each seed out of 20 is worth 5 percent. 19 times 5 is 95, and 18 times 5 is 90. The difference is one seed, and one seed can fail by chance.
maths.context: In the Freezer Test you put dry and soaked moong seeds in a freezer for a night. Then you count how many germinate. These are made-up counts for the two dry groups.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare groups, and knowing what one seed is worth tells you whether a difference means anything.

maths.problem: Look at the made-up Freezer Test chart. By how many percentage points did freezing lower the dry seeds? And the soaked seeds? What do the two answers tell you together?
maths.answer: Dry seeds: 5 points lower. Soaked seeds: 100 points lower. The harm from cold depends on whether the seed is wet.
maths.explain: Dry: 95 minus 90 is 5. Soaked: 100 minus 0 is 100. The same freezer did almost nothing to dry seeds and killed every soaked seed. So cold and water act together.

chart.title: Made-up Freezer Test results: percent germinated by day 5

maths.context: In the Freezer Test, four groups of 20 moong seeds were dry or soaked. Each group was kept on a shelf or in a freezer. This chart shows made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting within each pair shows the effect of one variable. Comparing the two differences shows that one variable changes what the other does.

maths.problem: A Rag Doll Test shows that a sack of paddy seed germinates at 80 percent. A farmer wants 2,000 seedlings. How many seeds should she sow?
maths.explain: 80 percent means 8 of every 10 seeds grow. 2,000 seedlings are 250 lots of 8. So she needs 250 lots of 10 seeds, which is 2,500.
maths.context: In the Rag Doll Test you roll 50 seeds in a wet cloth and count the strong seedlings. The count gives the germination percentage of a batch.
maths.why_maths: A germination percentage is only useful if you can turn it into the number of seeds to sow.

maths.problem: In Scoop and Guess, 80 percent of the seeds in the dabba are rajma. In a scoop of 5, which counts of rajma give a guess within 10 of 80 percent? In a scoop of 25?
maths.answer: In a scoop of 5: only 4 rajma. In a scoop of 25: 18, 19, 20, 21 or 22 rajma.
maths.explain: Out of 5, each seed is 20 percent, so 3, 4 and 5 rajma give 60, 80 and 100. Only 80 is within 10. Out of 25, each seed is 4 percent, so 18 to 22 rajma give 72 to 88. A bigger scoop has more ways to land close.
maths.context: In the game Scoop and Guess you take a few seeds from a dabba without looking. Then you guess what percent of all the seeds are rajma.
maths.why_maths: Working out what each seed is worth shows why a small sample jumps about. A big sample settles near the true value.

maths.problem: William Beal buried bottles of seeds in 1879. One bottle was opened in 2021, and the last is due in 2100. How long was each wait? How old will a child born in 2016 be in 2100?
maths.answer: 142 years and 221 years. The child will be 84.
maths.context: This is about the buried bottle test. A botanist buried bottles of weed seeds in 1879. Every few years, people dig up one bottle and see whether the seeds still germinate.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting years shows how far this test runs beyond one human life. That is why each scientist must hand the test on to the next.

maths.problem: In Three Jars, Three Weeks, the damp jar gave these made-up results. Between which two tests did germination fall most? A seed bank regrows seeds below 85 percent. By which test should these seeds have been regrown?
maths.answer: It fell most between week 1 and week 2. The seeds should have been regrown by week 1.
maths.explain: The first fall is 95 to 80, which is 15 points. The second is 80 to 45, which is 35 points. The third is 45 to 15, which is 30 points. The line first goes below 85 at week 1, when it reads 80.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out how long a seed can stay alive? This card tells the true story, including a claim that turned out to be wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1800s, many people in Europe believed that wheat from ancient Egyptian tombs had been sown and had grown. The grain was said to be 3,000 years old, and sellers offered 'mummy wheat' for gardens. Botanists then tested grain that truly came from tombs. Not one grain germinated. The grain was brown and brittle, and the embryos were dead. So how long can a seed really live? In 1879, William James Beal began a test to find out. He was a botanist at a college in Michigan in the United States. He filled 20 glass bottles with slightly damp sand. Into each bottle he mixed 50 seeds from each of 21 kinds of common weeds. He buried the bottles with their open mouths tilted down, so that rain could not fill them. Every few years a bottle was dug up and the seeds were sown. Beal knew the test would outlast him. In 2021, a team dug up a bottle after 142 years, and seeds of moth mullein still germinated. The last bottle is due to be opened in 2100.
how_we_found_out.who: William James Beal, an American botanist, and the scientists at Michigan State University who have carried on his test
how_we_found_out.when: The bottles were buried in 1879. A bottle was opened in 2021, after 142 years. The last one is due in 2100.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That wheat from Egyptian tombs, about 3,000 years old, could still grow. Tests on real tomb grain showed that it was dead. Beal's buried bottles then measured how long seeds really live, with seeds whose age was known.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in nineteenth-century clothes kneeling by a hole in a lawn, placing a glass bottle of sand in the ground with its open mouth tilted downwards.

roots.context: In this unit you froze dry seeds and soaked seeds, and you dried seeds that had started to wake. Here we ask what a waiting seed shows about life, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Freezer Test, dry moong lived through a night in the freezer, and soaked moong died. In No Going Back, moong who were dried after their roots came out died too. A dry seed can live through cold and drying that kill a seedling. So a plant is toughest as a dry seed, and once the root is out there is no way back.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a seed as the small, helpless start of a plant. We think of the grown plant as the strong one. Against cold and drought it is the other way round. The dry seed is the form in which a plant survives what no leaf or root can.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Freezer Test, dry moong from the freezer germinated about as well as dry moong from the shelf. Soaked moong from the freezer did not germinate. In No Going Back, seeds dried before the root appeared woke again. Seeds dried after the root appeared mostly did not. Seed banks freeze dry seeds for a hundred years. If your own results were different, write down what you saw.

three.who_am_i: Your body cannot stop and wait. Your heart must beat every second, and you must drink every day. You began as one cell that started growing and never paused.
three.what_is_life: Life does not have to keep moving to stay alive. A seed can become almost still for years, and then carry on from where they stopped.
three.what_is_this_world: The soil under a field, a park or a flower pot holds living seeds that nobody sowed. The ground is full of plants who are waiting.

roots.thread: A dry seed and a growing plant are one living being in two forms. One form is hard, dry and still, and can wait for a thousand years. The other form is soft, wet and growing, and cannot wait for a week without water. Every flowering plant passes from stillness to growth and back to stillness, as seed, plant and seed again. Many sages taught that stillness is the source that all moving things come from and return to.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to split a banyan seed and say what is inside. The boy sees nothing at all. His father says that the great banyan tree stands up out of that fine essence which he cannot see.
teachings.link: A dry seed shows nothing when you open one: no movement, no growth. Yet the whole plant is there, held still. The Upanishad uses the seed to teach about the self, which science does not test.

teachings.teaching: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, the grain stays alone. If the grain dies, a great harvest follows.
teachings.link: A seed that germinates stops being a seed for good, as No Going Back showed. A seed that never wakes stays one seed. The verse uses this to teach about giving oneself, which is a teaching and not a finding.

teachings.teaching: All things rise and grow, and each one returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness.
teachings.link: A plant's year ends in seeds, which are the plant made still. From that stillness the next growth begins.

science.text: In a dry seed, the inside of each cell sets into a glassy solid in which molecules can hardly move. This is why the seed's chemistry almost stops.
Tardigrades, some mosses and some ferns can also dry out, wait for years and become active again. This ability has arisen in many branches of life.
Whether a very dry, very cold seed has any activity at all, or none, is not known. Any activity is too small to measure so far.

other_view.who: Some biologists who study dried and frozen living things
other_view.view: Life is a set of activities: feeding, respiring, repairing, growing. A fully dry seed does none of them, so at that time the seed is not living. The seed is a very well kept set of parts that can start living again. On this view, 'alive' and 'dead' are not enough, and a third word is needed for the dry seed.

practice.title: Still as a seed
practice.say: Hold one dry seed in your closed hand. Sit as still as you can for one minute. Do not move a finger. Now notice what did not stop. Your breath went in and out. Your heart kept beating. The seed in your hand has been stiller than that for months. Open your hand and look at the seed for three slow breaths.
practice.kid: Hold a dry seed in your fist. Sit very still for one minute. Notice your breath. Notice your heartbeat. You could not stop them. The seed has been still for months. Open your hand and look.

ask: A lotus seed did almost nothing for 1,300 years, and then grew. What was the seed during all those years?
Once the root is out, a seed cannot go back. If you were a seed, what would you want to be sure of before you woke?
You cannot become still and wait, as a seed can. What can a seed do that you cannot, and what can you do that a seed cannot?

playtest: Read through step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but have not been tried at home. Please treat the expected results as likely and not certain. The Freezer Test (core) needs 80 whole moong, four plates, cloths and a freezer. Dry moong should germinate almost fully after a night in the freezer, and soaked moong should not. If the freezer is weak or the soaked seeds sat in a thick heap, a few soaked seeds may live. No Going Back (core) needs 65 moong and a fan or an airy shelf. Seeds dried before a root shows should grow again. Seeds dried with a root of about 1 centimetre should mostly fail, though a few may grow a new root. In damp monsoon weather the drying takes a day longer. Three Jars, Three Weeks needs three jars with tight lids. The damp jar usually grows mould, so a grown-up opens the jar by a window. In a cool room the seeds in damp air die more slowly. The project then needs four or five weeks. If water drips onto the pouch, some seeds may sprout inside the jar. The step says to write that down. The Rag Doll Test works with any whole seeds, and chana and lobia need one more day. Four Days, Four Drawings (core) needs 8 kabuli chana. Read the Five Jars (core) needs only a pencil, and its table is made up. Scoop and Guess (core) needs 45 rajma and 25 kabuli chana, and one child can play it alone. The Power Cut needs three ice cubes. In a cool room the bare cube may take longer than 90 minutes to melt. Nothing needs a garden. Facts to treat with care: the ages of the lotus seed (about 1,300 years) and the date seed (about 2,000 years) come from carbon dating and are rounded. The numbers of samples at Svalbard and at India's National Genebank grow every year. The Bible, Upanishad and Tao Te Ching passages are paraphrases. Two of the three videos have no address yet.
